That the Assembly express its deepest appreciation for the hardworking staff in the Office of the Stated Clerk, especially for Mr. Ross E. Cook, Business Administrator, who will be retiring before the end of the year, for Mrs. Laurel De Bert, Administrative Assistant, for Chaplain J Robert Fiol, Assistant to the Stated Clerk, and for Mr. Jerry Kornegay, Director of the PCA Historical Center in St. Louis, who has resigned his position to move to Knoxville, Tennessee Adopted TE Bill Fox, Chairman of the Administrative Committee, presented a plaque to RE Ross Cook, AC Business Administrator, on behalf of the Assembly, due to his retirement later this year. 8 That the 26th General Assembly express its gratitude to the Lord for the good spirit of cooperation among the Coordinators, Directors, and Presidents of the committees and agencies, and pray that this spirit continues to grow Adopted 9. The Committee refers the following to the General Assembly Committee of commissioners for the pc .A Foundation: (See 26-65, III, 4 and 6, p. 220 For final disposition) That GA amend the Corporate Bylaws of the PCA, Article VI, Section 5, the first two paragraphs as follows: “The Board of Directors of Presbyterian Church in America Foundation, Inc., shall consist of ten (10) members: (a) Five (5) Six (6) members in classes elected through the standard nomination and election procedures (the “at large members”); and (b) one (1) member from each of the following permanent committees or board of trustees of the agencies: (1) Christian Education and Publications, {2-) Covenant College, (3- 2) Covenant Theological Seminary, (4 3) Mission to the World, and (# 4) Mission to North America (the “Appointed Members”). the chairman of the board of directors of Presbyterian Church in America Foundation, Inc. shall bean at large member. The at-large members shall serve for four (4) year terms, and shall be divided into four (4) classes, each class being as nearly equal in number as possible, so that the terms of approximately one-fourth of the at-large members shall expire each year. Directors shall be eligible for reelection to a secondfour-year term after which there must be a one-year interval before further election. 10. That the 26th GA accept the invitation from Evangel Presbytery to host the 30th General Assembly in June 2002 in the Birmingham area subject to available suitable facilities. Adopted 11. That the 26th GA respond to Overture 8 from Heritage Presbytery “Cease Publishing Private Information in Yearbook’’ by referring it to the AC with instructions to the Stated Clerk to review with legal counsel and other knowledgeable persons the questions of privacy raised, and to report to the October 1998 meeting of AC in order to implement any appropriate recommendations both for the AC and for other committees and agencies. Adopted

“Cease Publishing Private Information in Yearbook” Whereas, the PCA Yearbook annually contains enough personal information about PCA ministers to potentially severely compromise privacy of its ministers to persons of ill will, Whereas, in years past such information was gathered prior to modem privacy problems. Whereas, material gathered from the PCA Yearbook together with other reasonably available information could significantly compromise the financial integrity of ministers by persons o fill will, Whereas, this publishing this information provides no significant useful legitimate purpose, Therefore be it resolved, that the General Assembly instruct the Stated Clerk’s Office to cease gathering or publishing mother’s maiden name and location of birth of ministers, And to review other data gathered for the Yearbook and cease publishing information about churches, agencies or ministers that is of little use and may be potentially damaging. And that the General Assembly instruct the other committees and agencies to review their gathering of and distributing of personal information No personal information should be gathered unless there is significant legitimate purpose. If so gathered, it must be kept confidential. Attested by: /s/ Bruce B Howes, Stated Clerk 12. That Overture 6 from Eastern Carolina Presbytery “Permit Vendors to Sell at GA Booths” be answered in the negative Adopted Grounds: 1. Monitoring local government requirements for sales taxes and business licenses for exhibitors would be cumbersome for the AC staff 2. Monitoring the sales items of the exhibitors to ensure that the items offered for sale meet appropriate doctrinal and other standards, and that vendors are not selling the same items as the CE&P Bookstore would be an additional burden for the AC staff.

“Permit vendors to sell at ga Booths” Whereas, the General Assembly, in addition to its work as a court, also provides a forum for the encouragement of the commissioners in attendance; Whereas, the General Assembly from the beginning has permitted vendors to set up booths to display their materials, Whereas, this practice provides a valuable service in giving commissioners an opportunity to see materials and talk to company representatives which might otherwise be difficult to do; Whereas, these vendors pay a significant fee to have such booths, Whereas, only the PCA Bookstore is allowed to sell materials at the Assembly and other vendors are not permitted to sell their goods and services; Whereas, the PCA bookstore does not carry many of the goods which vendors would be willing to make available; Whereas, there have been vendors who no longer display their goods and services because this policy greatly hinders their recouping their costs in having such a booth, Whereas, the present policy works to the disadvantage and inconvenience of the commissioners at the General Assembly; It is moved that the General Assembly direct the Permanent Committee on Administration to allow vendors to sell those goods and services at the General Assembly which are either not available through the PCA Bookstore booth or having been available at the booth have sold out. Adopted at the Winter Stated Meeting of Eastern Carolina Presbytery, January 24, 1998. Attested by: /s/ Austin Leake, Stated Clerk

“Repudiate response of irc to investigation of 1997” Whereas, our Constitution reminds us that the requirements of the Ninth Commandment include “the preserving and promoting of truth between man and man, and the good name of our neighbor, as well as our own, appearing and standing for the truth, love and care of our own good name, and defending it when need requireth, . . (Larger Catechism, Q/A 144), and that among those things which are forbidden by the Ninth Commandment are “undue silence in a just cause, and holding our peace when iniquity calleth for either a reproof from ourselves, or complaint to others . (Larger Catechism, Q/A 145), and Whereas, Northeast Presbytery joined with three sister presbyteries in overturing the 25th General Assembly to investigate fully the actions of the Interchurch Relations Committee (IRC); and Whereas, the reason behind the call for said investigation was that, primci facie, the IRC had failed to carry out the directive of a previous General Assembly, and Whereas, in issuing this call for investigation, none of the presbyteries questioned the motives of the IRC in its actions, and Whereas, in responding to these overtures, the IRC did attack the motives of the presbyteries which had expressed this concern, and Whereas, the IRC employed harsh language in describing the presbyteries and their overtures (“The IRC frankly is offended by these overtures. . Not only do they contain factual errors but also what could be described as deliberate distortions of the truth We maintain that Christian charity, the command of love to ‘believe all things’ (1 Corinthians 13:7), a concern for the effects of false accusations, for ‘the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity, and it is set on fire by hell’ (James 3:6), a recognition that the works of the flesh include ‘contentions, . . dissentions, factions’ (Galatians 5:20), and a reminder of the admonition to ‘avoid foolish disputes, contentions, for they are unprofitable and useless’ (Titus 3 :9), ought to have tempered our brothers’ actions”); and Whereas, the IRC’s report alleges that there were numerous factual errors in at least one of the overtures to the General Assembly; and Whereas, there were no substantive errors in any of these overtures, and Whereas, to the contrary, there were numerous factual errors which the IRC committed in its report to the 25th General Assembly (see attached sheets), and Whereas, having taken umbrage when the fraternal delegate of the christian Reformed Church used the same terminology of the IRC report (“factual errors deliberate distortions of the truth. . .”) to express profound disagreement with the IRC’s evaluation of his denomination, the 25th General Assembly defended its reputation by spreading on the record a response to the delegate’s remarks, and Whereas, the 25th General Assembly did not likewise protect the reputations of four of its constituent presbyteries; and Whereas, Northeast Presbytery frankly is offended by having been castigated by a Committee of the General Assembly; Now Therefore be it resolved, that Northeast Presbytery hereby overtures the 26th General Assembly to repudiate the IRC’s response to these overtures to the last Assembly, and to request the resignation of any current members of their c who approved o for helped to write the 1997 report. EVALUATING THE INTERCHURCH RELATIONS REPORT TO THE 1997 GENERAL ASSEMBLY There are discrepancies between the IRC Report to the 1997 General Assembly and statements made at and actions taken at NAPARC [NOTE: unless otherwise noted, the references are to the 1997 Commissioners’ Handbook]. IRC Report The report states that a letter was received from the Christian Reformed Church (CRC), and says: “The Committee did not respond to this letter At their meeting on September 1996, the letter from Dr. Engelhard was viewed as the response of the CRC to the action of the 23rd General Assembly, the letter did not seem to need a reply Later, it became clear that Dr Engelhard expected a response. . .” [p 807, lines 26-28], FACT: Immediately after the NAPARC meeting, Dr Bill Edgar, a member of the Interchurch Relations Committee, stated that “we never received” the letter from the CRC Synod, “probably because of the US mail” failing to deliver it [P&R News, Fall 1996], IRC Report The report says that “[l]ater on in the Assembly [sic], under new business, the PCA raised the question with regard to the CRC” [p. 813, lines 4- 5] FACT: The delegation first raised the issue under Communications on the previous day [Minutes, 1996 NAPARC meeting], IRC Report The Committee says that “[t]he matter was put to a vote as to whether the matter was properly before the Council since the Bylaws had just been amended to permit suspension before termination” [p. 813, lines 25-27], FACT There was never any discussion at NAPARC as to the propriety of the motion to suspend in contrast to a motion to terminate membership. The question raised had to do with whether this new business came under new Bylaws which deal with how to handle new business, including its timeliness [Minutes, 1996 NAPARC meeting]. There are discrepancies between the IRC Report to the 1997 General Assembly and the account gleaned from the 21s1 General Assembly minutes IRC Report Dealing with “some history,” the report notes that the 20th General Assembly (1992) “instructed the IRC to prepare documentation regarding the CRC’s actions in such areas as ‘the view of Scripture, the toleration of beliefs in evolution and homosexuality, and the treatment of brethren who have stood against these modernist trends’. . This was a far greater task than perhaps the GA understood when it ordered the report and consequently the IRC was unable to bring its report to the 21s1 General Assembly: [pp. 814-815], FACT: In 1993, the Committee noted that the action of the 20th GA regarding the CRC had been taken before the Assembly had heard from the cr c regarding the actions of the 1992 Synod. The Committee recommended that the 21st GA communicate to the CRC its thanksgiving to God that it did not open the church offices of minister, elder and evangelist to women. The Committee then stated: “It is the strong feeling that it would be inappropriate and even offensive to the CRC, for the PCA to initiate an investigation into the internal affairs of another denomination, especially when that denomination is in the process of seeking to resolve their problems and debates. We wish them well” [M21GA, p. 392], IRC Report This year’s report states that the effect of adopting an overture which called the CRC to repentance “sent the ICR in a search to verify the alleged deviations listed in the overture” [p 815, lines 11-12], FACT: The 1993 General Assembly voted that the IRC should “comply with instructions given by the 20th General Assembly” to “prepare documentation with regard to the Christian Reformed Church” [M21GA, p. 68], The IRC’s rationale with regard to its action regarding the CRC’s relationship to NAPARC is dubious at best IRC Report: This year’s report states that at the 1996 meeting of NAPARC, “the PCA delegation brought a motion to suspend the CRC and thus began the process toward eventual expulsion of the CRC.” It then lists several reasons why it took this action. “First, while suspension is not necessary for removal of a denomination, it was widely assumed that this was the place to begin” [p 816, lines 7ff|. FACT: The vast majority of the members on the 1995 IRC committee of Commissioners, which brought the recommendation to the floor, have expressed that there was no such assumption on their part [P&R News, Fall, 1996], The Committee of Commissioners had decided to ask the Assembly to wait until the 1996 NAPARC meeting, so as to give the CRC one more year to repent. But apart from that repentance, the definite intention was to terminate the CRC’s membership, swiftly. IRC Report “Our own processes of discipline in the PCA anticipate a progression of judgments which might lead to repentance on the part of the accused” [p. 816, lines 11-13] FACT: It is not true that PCA discipline mandates that suspension precede excommunication. Although that may usually be the case, a church court may proceed to inflict the highest censure immediately upon trial [for example, see BCO 37-9], IRC Report The Committee gave its second reason: “the CRC is due to revisit the issue [of women’s ordination] in the year 2000. . [A] motion to remove (skipping suspension) would run into strong arguments that in fairness to the CRC, their own review process must be honored before the women in office decision can be considered irrevocable” [p. 816, lines 14-19], FACT This reason appears to many to be a mere excuse and no reason at all. It documents that the IRC did not carry out the intention of the General Assembly. Moreover, the IRC’s own report stated that “no one expects the CRC to return to its earlier position forbidding women in office” [p 816, lines 14-15] - which reality could very well answer any argument about the CRC not having completed its review process IRC Report The third reason given in the report was that “the IRC felt that a ‘grand gesture’ of a motion to remove the CRC from NAP ARC would almost certainly fail, as at the moment the OPC and the CRC are in the process of discussing the issue. Thus it was felt that a motion to suspend could in fact gather enough support to pass Then, when practical, certainly no later than the 2000 meeting, the process could be completed with a vote to remove the CRC” [p 816, lines 19-23] FACT: There is a significant change in verb tense: the Committee “felt” (past tense), because the OPC and CRC “are in the process of discussing” (Present tense) the matter in point of fact, the OPC and CRC were NOT discussing the matter when the 1996 NAP ARC meeting took place. Therefore, it is questionable how much effect their discussions could have had on the action of the IRC delegation. there are problems with the account by their co fits processing of the question of CRC membership in NAP ARC. IRC Report The Committee, in dealing with several overtures, contends that the “allegation” that the IRC did not make a motion to remove the CRC from NAP ARC is “misleading” [p 817, line 4], FACT: As their own report demonstrates, they admit that they did NOT make such a motion [p. 816, lines 7ff| There might be any number of reasons why they did not - but, as an historical fact and a matter of record, the delegation did NOT make that motion. it is not an “allegation” - it is simply a statement of fact. IRC Report: With regard to the matter of CRC membership in NAP ARC “almost. . not mak[ing] it onto the agenda,” the IRC begins by admitting that “it did not do everything right. members of the delegation assumed that the matter was ‘live’ as old business. Ideally the matter should have been communicated to NAPARC as an agenda request four weeks before the meeting. It was also understood that the OPC was bringing a similar motion. At the critical moment when planning ought to have been done, the committee chairman was forced to resign his chairmanship due to personal and family needs and was himself unable to attend the meeting. This placed the committee in a temporary state of confusion and some matters were not carried out as well as they might have been” [p. 817, lines 1Off], FACT: This matter was not on the NAPARC agenda. (At least four distinct advance notices for the meeting were sent out.) The 1995 General Assembly adopted the motion to use all due process to remove the CRC at the 1996 NAPARC meeting; thereby affording the Committee over a year to figure out how to carry out the Assembly’s mandate. FACT: Note also the appeal to the OPC. as the chairman of the OPC ecumenicity committee has stated, no one talked to his Committee [P&R News, Spring 1997], so it was impossible for the PCA’s Committee to know what the OPC position was going to be in relation to making a …

source: OVERTURE 22 From the Presbytery of the Ascension
body: “Require IRC to Demonstrate Errors in Overtures to 25th GA” Whereas, our Constitution reminds us that the requirements of the Ninth Command include “the preserving and promoting of truth between man and man, and the good name of our neighbor, as well as our own; appearing and standing for the truth,...love and care for our own good name, and defending it when need requireth,...” [Larger Catechism, Q/A 144], and that among those things which are forbidden by the Ninth Commandment are “undue silence in a just cause, and holding our peace when iniquity calleth for either a reproof from ourselves, or complaint to others . .” [Larger Catechism Q/A 145]; and Whereas, the Presbytery of the Ascension joined with three sister presbyteries in overturing the 25th General Assembly to investigate fully the actions of the Interchurch Relations Committee (IRC); and Whereas, the reason behind the call for said investigation was that, prima facie, their chad failed to carryout the directive of a previous General Assembly; and Whereas, in issuing this call for investigation, none of the presbyteries questioned the motives of the irc in its actions, and Whereas, in responding to these overtures, the IRC did attack the motives of the presbyteries which had expressed this concern, and Whereas, the IRC employed harsh language in describing the presbyteries and their overtures (“The IRC frankly is offended by these overtures. . Not only do they contain factual errors but also what could be described as deliberate distortions of the truth. . .We maintain that Christian charity, the command of love to ‘believe all things’ (1 Corinthians 13:7), a concern for the effects of false accusations, for ‘the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity. . and it is set on fire by hell’ (James 3:6), a recognition that the works of the flesh include ‘contentions,.. dissensions, factions’ (Galatians 5,20) and a reminder of the admonition to ‘avoid foolish disputes,. . . contentions. . . for they are unprofitable and useless’ (Titus 3:9), ought to have tempered our brothers, actions”); and Whereas, the IRC’s report alleges that there were numerous factual errors in at least one of the overtures to the General Assembly; and Whereas, there we reno substantive errors demonstrated in any of these overtures, Therefore be it resolved that the Presbytery of the Ascension ask the Interchurch Relations Committee through the 26th General Assembly to demonstrate the errors mentioned in their report to the 25th General Assembly or to apologize to the presbyteries involved Adopted at the April 1998 stated meeting of the Presbytery of the Ascension on April 25, 1998 Attested by: /s/ Frederick R Neikirk, Stated Clerk

“Change boundaries of northern california presbytery to include Additional Counties in Nevada and Utah” Whereas, the Presbytery of Northern California has shown itself both aggressive and effective in church planting, adding 10 churches and missions from 1991 through 1996 and over 1,000 members, and Whereas, three of the Northern California Presbytery’s new missions in the last four years a RE in the state of Utah, which is outside the boundaries of any presbytery, and Whereas, the boundaries of northern california presbytery already include the nevada counties of Douglas, Carson City, Storey, and Lyon and the nevada counties of Washoe, Churchill, Eureka, White Pine, Elko, Humboldt, Lander and Pershing are naturally connected by Interstate 80 and US Route 50, Therefore be it resolved that the 26th General Assembly ADD THE STATE OF UTAH AND THE FOLLOWING COUNTIES IN THE STATE OF NEVADA: Washoe, Churchill, Eureka, White Pine, Elko, Humboldt, Lander and Pershing to the boundaries of the Northern California Presbytery. adopted at the stated meeting of northern california presbytery on february 11, 1998. Attested by: /s/ Arthur R. Schick, Stated Clerk

“Deny Enlarging Northern California Presbytery” Whereas, from its beginning, the Presbyterian Church in America has sought to reach out to the entire nation, and Whereas, the PCA’s philosophy in doing so has been to restrict geographical boundaries of presbyteries to a reasonable size and to allow all of the presbyteries and churches to have responsibility for spreading the gospel in the destitute areas of the church, and Whereas, the 1984 General Assembly stated: “That our presbyteries be encouraged to limit their boundaries to those geographic areas for which they are able to take meaningful responsibility in evangelism and church development, leaving other areas for orchestrated action of all presbyteries working together through the General Assembly”; and Whereas, Central Georgia Presbytery ordained a man in March 1998 to be a church planter in the Provo, Utah, area, and Whereas, Central Georgia Presbytery, in ordaining this man to undertake this work, was acting in full accord with encouragement of the General Assembly and the examples of other Presbyteries, and Whereas, Northern California Presbytery has overtured the General Assembly to extend its boundaries so that Nevada and all of Utah would be included within its bounds, thus adding close to 200,000 square miles to its territory, and Whereas, if this overture from Northern California were approved, no other presbytery could lawfully plant churches in this vast area, and Whereas, Northern California is a small presbytery numerically, as is evident from the latest available denominational statistics (1,166 communicant members, thus ranking 43rd out of 49 Anglo presbyteries in communicant strength; total giving to the presbytery from the churches was $21,247.00, thus ranking 39th out of 49 Anglo presbyteries), and Whereas, as adopted by the General Assembly, the minimal ideal for a presbytery is to have at least three churches with 125 communicant members, and according to the latest denominational statistics, Northern California has only two such churches; and Whereas, the ideal boundaries for a presbytery, as set forth by the General Assembly, include driving distances of no more than two and a half hours, and Whereas, the driving distance across Nevada and Utah along Interstate 80 is more than 600 miles, and Whereas, the driving distance between the Nevada-California border and San Francisco is another 200 miles; and Whereas, if the Northern California overture were adopted, Northern California’s boundaries would stretch about 4,000 miles, from the international dateline in the middle of the pacific ocean to the rocky Mountains, and Whereas, Utah has more in common with Colorado than with California, as is evident culturally and geographically and as reflected in the fact that the old skyline synod of the presbyterian church in the united states of America encompasses Colorado and Utah. Now therefore, be it resolved, that Central Georgia Presbytery hereby overtures the 26th General Assembly to do the following: Deny the request from Northern California Presbytery to extend its boundaries so that the denomination may continue to bring its entire resources to be aron the destitute regions of the Nation. Adopted at the Spring Meeting of Central Georgia Presbytery on April 14, 1998 Attested by: Julian H. Davis, Stated Clerk

source: OVERTURE 7 From the Presbytery of Central Florida
body: “Change Boundaries to Establish North Florida Presbytery” Whereas, a presbytery confined to a smaller geographic area can lead to more efficient oversight and cooperation. As our presbytery group has grown larger, it has experienced a declining spirit of unity and has become nessarily less personal Whereas, the history of Central Florida Presbytery supports the notion that a healthy division can produce growth. Whereas, greater regionalization will allow for greater focus on the unique needs of a particular area Whereas, our present presbytery’s geographic expanse is too large for efficient involvement especially when Saturday meetings are involved. Whereas, smaller presbyteries should equal shorter meetings. Whereas, newer presbyteries will allow for fresh approach and possibly a better approach to “doing” presbytery. Whereas, greater geographic ownership in church planting should lead to greater involvement and investment. Whereas, this division meets all the guidelines established by the PCA for the formation of a new presbytery. Therefore be it resolved that General Assembly at its July 1998 meeting divide the presbytery of central florida and form the north florida Presbytery to include all churches and missions found within the borders of Hamilton, Suwanee, Lafayette, Dixie, Columbia, Baker, Union, Alachua, Gilchrist, Nassua, Duval, Bradford, Clay, Putnam, St. Johns, Flagler counties and churches and missions affected are, Christ Church (Jacksonville), Northshore (Jacksonville), Ortega (Jacksonville), Pinewood (Middleburg), Ponte Vedra (Ponte Vedra), Redeemer (Jacksonville), Westminster (Jacksonville), Cross Creek Mission (Fruit Cove), Community (Live Oak), Faith (Gainesville, Good News (St. Augustine), Grace Mission (Palm Coast) and Community (McIntosh, within the borders of Marion county). adopted at the stated meeting of presbytery of central florida on january 20, 1998 Attested by: /si Donald L. Mountan, Stated Clerk

“Investigate Worship Practices in Mission Churches in Utah” Whereas, Central Georgia Presbytery ordained a man in March 1998 to be a church planter in the Provo, Utah, area, and Whereas, it has now come to the attention of central georgia presbytery that some of the PCA mission churches in the utah area are introducing into worship many questionable practices, including what might be called an mtv format of rock music, film clips, and video, and Whereas, affirming the legitimacy of such practices has been made a test for service by some in the western region of our denomination, including those in positions of authority; and Whereas, one of the prime examples of the type of ministry with which our evangelist would have had to work is the New Song Salt Lake; and Whereas, New Song Salt Lake’s approach to ministry can be seen in its internet website which featured pictures of the pastor and pastoral assistant on Beavis and Butthead torsos; and Whereas, New Song Salt Lake regularly employed alternative rock music as part of “public worship”, and Whereas, among the lyrics which have been offered in “public worship” are the following: “What will people think when they hear that I’m a Jesus freak?/What will people do when they find that that’s true?/I don’t really care if they label me a Jesus freak/There is no disguising the truth”, and Whereas, at worship services film clips from secular movies, such as Soul Food, have been shown, including extremely offensive profanity, and Whereas, at least two people, including a youth worker from a congregation of the liberal Presbyterian Church (United states of America), have been regularly leading worship and supplying the pulpit at New Song Salt lake even though neither of them has regular ministerial credentials which would qualify them for that work, and Whereas, many in the PCA would be offended to know that their benevolence dollars are being used to promote the type of worship as described above, Now therefore, be it resolved, that Central Georgia Presbytery hereby overtures the 26th General Assembly to do the following: 1 Investigate whether or not such practices have been promoted as a regular part of the worship of PCA Missions in Utah, and 2. investigate whether or not acceptance of such practices has become, whether implicitly or explicitly, a requirement for service in the western region of our denomination, and 3. Remove from employment any MNA personnel who have in any way encouraged the type of “worship” displayed at New Song Salt Lake, or who have encouraged making or affirming the legitimacy of such a test for service, or who, knowing what was going on, acquiesced in it by failing to bring such to the attention of the church-at-large Adopted at the Spring Stated Meeting of Central Georgia Presbytery on April 14,1998 Attested by: /s/ Julian H Davis, Stated Clerk

source: OVERTURE 28 From the Presbytery of Grace
body: “Expression of support for overtures 16 and 17 Re Enlarging Pacific Presbytery and Investigating Worship Practices” Whereas, Grace Presbytery is interested in the work of the church-at-large, and Whereas, we are part of a connectional church which seeks to spread into the entire United States of America; and Whereas, questionable worship practices have apparently been introduced into various mission work sunder the sponsorship of the denominational Mission to North America (MNA) Committee, including the use of alternative rock music and film clips from secular movies; and Whereas, at least one of the reasons why our denomination was formed in 1973 out of the Southern Presbyterian Church is because of the experimental worship that was being sponsored by the Southern Presbyterian home missions board, and Whereas, the continuation of such worship practices in our mission works threatens denominational unity and is offensive to many in the church who contribute benevolence dollars to the MNA Committee, and Whereas, Northern California Presbytery has overtured the General Assembly to expand its bounds to include most of Nevada and all of Utah so that no other presbytery could plant churches in that area; and Whereas, this expansion of territory could have a detrimental effect on the efforts by the church as a whole in the planting of traditional churches in that vast area, and Whereas, one of our sister presbyteries, Central Georgia, has adopted two overtures with regard to these matters; Now Therefore be it resolved, that Grace Presbytery hereby expresses its sympathy with and support for the overtures from Central Georgia and urges the 26th Presbyterian Church in America General Assembly to adopt them adopted by the presbytery of grace in its 91st Stated Meeting on the 12th of May, 1998 Attested by: /s/ Eugene C. Case, Stated Clerk

“Amend RAO 4, Adding New Section 18, Allowing Nominations From Committees and Agencies” Whereas, Article VI of the Bylaws of the PCA permits the Boards of Trustees of Insurance, Annuities & Relief, Covenant College; Covenant Theological Seminary and the PCA Foundation to make requests to the Presbyteries to nominate specific men to their respective boards, and Whereas, article vi of the bylaws of the PCA permits the boards of trustees of Covenant College, Covenant Theological Seminary and the PCA Foundation to submit to the General Assembly Nominating Committee letters of recommendation concerning particular nominees for their respective boards, and Whereas, past actions of the general assemblies of the PCA in approving the procedures mentioned above presumes that these Boards have good and valid reasons to be given such permission, and Whereas, the Bible clearly teaches that there should be no partiality shown in the work of the church (e.g. Deut. 1:17, 10:17; Mark 10:35-45; 1 Timothy 5:21), and Whereas, the Book of Church Order (14-1-3) spells out this Biblical principal when it states: “The work of the Church as set forth in the Great Commission is one work, being implemented at the General Assembly level through equally essential committees” (emphasis added), and Whereas, other Committees and Boards of the PCA may feel that permission to communicate with Presbyteries and with the General Assembly Nominating Committee would better enable them to carry out the duties assigned to them by the General Assembly, Therefore Be it Resolved that NEW RIVER PRESBYTERY, meeting at New Martinsville, West Virginia on the 15th day of November, 1997, does hereby overture the 26th General Assembly to add a new Section 4-18 to the rules of assembly Operation, as follows: “Any Committee or Agency of the PCA whose members are elected by the General Assembly through the report of the assembly Nominating Committee may, at its own discretion, make requests to the Presbyteries to nominate specific men to said Committee/Agency and may submit to the Assembly Nominating Committee letters of recommendation concerning particular nominees from the Presbyteries. such requests and recommendations must be made by vote of the full committee/board of trustees and signed by the Chairman or his designee. Notwithstanding these requests and recommendations, the Presbyteries remain free to nominate men of their own choice and the nominating committee is free to present nominees to the General Assembly of their own choice.” 2. That Overture 23 from Tennessee Valley Presbytery be answered in the affirmative with the following revision. Adopted

source: OVERTURE 23 From the Tennessee Valley Presbytery
body: “Amend RAO 14-7,c,3 to Require Citing Specific BCO Reference for Exceptions taken by CRPR” Whereas, during the proceedings of the General Assembly when Exceptions of Substance are noted without the citation of specific Scriptural or BCO references, confusion of interpretation causes a lack of definitive action, and Whereas, the endorsement of such an Exception to Substance could represent careless activity on the part of the General Assembly; Therefore we respectfully request that Rules of Assembly Operation 14-9,c,3 be amended to require that whenever Exceptions of Substance are reported to the General Assembly by the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records, the report shall in every case, include the Committee’s rationale for the exception of Substance. In addition, whenever an apparent violation of the constitution of the PCA is the reason for the exception of the Substance, the Committee must cite specific Scriptural and BCO references, that RAO 14-7.c.3 be amended by adding after the words “General Assembly," the phrase “which presentation shall include citation of any relevant Scriptural and or Constitutional references, and provide the Committee's rationale for finding the exception of Substance. ”

“Erect a Study Committee on Exegetical, Hermeneutical and Theological Interpretation of Genesis 1-3” Whereas, genesis is the fountainhead of the doctrines grace and the covenants of promise. The apostle Paul bases his exposition of the imputation of the righteousness of the Second Adam to God’s elect on the federal headship of the first Adam over the entire human race. Romans 5:17, “For if by one man’s offence death reigned by one; much more they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ.” 1 Corinthians 15:45, “And so it is written, The first Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam (was made) a quickening spirit.” Whereas, interpretations of genesis 1-3 have a direct bearing on the interpretation of New Testament passages. For example, Genesis 2:17, “But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die ”, has a direct bearing on the interpretation of the New Testament passage regarding rule of death in Romans 5:14, “Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam’s transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come.” Whereas, The PCA Digest: Position Papers 1973-1993 of the Presbyterian Church in America does not specifically address allowable exceptions to the standards regarding the exegetical, hermeneutical and theological interpretations of Genesis 1-3. Whereas, Examinations of ruling elders, candidates, licentiates and ordained ministers by Sessions and Presbyteries both in the areas of biblical knowledge and theology require clear criteria regarding the allowable exceptions to the standards regarding the exegetical, hermeneutical and theological interpretations of genesis 1-3. Whereas, the thursday evening session of the 25th General Assembly pointedly debated in the report of the review of presbytery records the allowable exceptions to the standards regarding the exegetical, hermeneutical and theological interpretations of Genesis 1-3. It is an issue affecting the peace of the church. Whereas, the proper context fora doctrinal debate is in response to a report of a study committee’s draft of allowable exceptions to the standards regarding the exegetical, hermeneutical and theological interpretations of Genesis 1-3. Therefore, be it resolved, that Central Carolina Presbytery hereby overtures the 26* General Assembly to form a two year study committee funded with a budget of $10,000 to clarify parameters for exceptions to the standards regarding the exegetical, hermeneutical, and theological interpretations of Genesis 1-3.

“Appoint Study Committee on Creation” Whereas, the culture in which we live has been permeated with evolutionary thinking which is an unbiblical and anti-scientific theory of origins, Whereas, the issue of the veracity of god and his word are under fierce attack in our day, Whereas, it is the position of Westminster Presbytery that the Bible teaches a six day creation, with day defined as an approximately 24 hour period of time and that Genesis 2 teaches not another creation account but a more detailed account of Genesis 1 regarding the creation of man on the 6th day and the creation of the garden of Eden, Whereas, westminster presbytery holds that the word of god teaches a 24 hour day because: 1. In Genesis 1:14-19, the Lord God describes the function of the sun and the moon to delineate the day from the night, this referring to a portion of a 24 hour period of time, 2. Where the recurring phrase evening and morning occur in the Scriptures, it always refers to an approximately 24 hour period of time, 3. the reason given for observance of the 4th commandment in Exodus 20:11 is base dona 24 hour day view of creation Whereas, Westminster Presbytery holds that a 24 hour view of the days of creation is absolutely necessary if, 1. we are to have a biblical view that man is a spiritual (hands on) creation of God, Genesis 2:7, 21, 22, 2. we are to have a biblical view of the origin of death, Genesis 2:16, 17, Romans 6:23, Whereas, Westminster Presbytery rejects the following positions as examples of views out of accord with the Scripture which has been carefully and accurately exposited in our standards, the WCF, WLC, and WSC: 1 The ‘gap theory’ which calls for a gap of time before or between the days of creation, 2. The so called ‘day age theory’ which holds that the term day in Genesis 1 does not refer to 24 hours, but to long epochs of time, 3. The ‘poetic’ view of Genesis 1 sometimes known as the ‘framework hypothesis’ view which maintains that Genesis 1 does not state history but an allegorical or symbolic declaration that somehow God, with the details not being important, created the world. According to this view, the facts and the order of events of creation are obscured by the poetic, illustrative language of the text. Comments on these views: Note that there is absolutely nothing in the text to even hint, let alone explicitly declare these views. All through the Scripture the historicity of creation is referred to Examples include: Exodus 20:8-11, Deuteronomy 5:12-15, Psalm 33:6-9, Psalm 104:1-6, Matthew 19:4-6, Romans 5:12-21, Romans 4:17, Hebrews 11:3, 1 Timothy 2:11-14, 1 Corinthians 3:8-12, I Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-47 This does great violence to the clear teaching of Scripture. These views appear to be held merely to seek to accommodate the evolutionary view of origins that postulates millions of years for the earth to appear as it does If consistently applied throughout the Word of God, this hermeneutic renders Scripture uninterpretable in an objective, meaningful way. these views of scripture are perpetrated by the neo-orthodox liberals of our day. we repudiate it as heresy. it is the same method of perverting and twisting the Scriptures that has been championed by denominations to “justify” the ordination of women to ecclesiastical office, to commend and approve of homosexuality as an acceptable lifestyle, and to permit sodomites to hold ecclesiastical offices. It is the same hermeneutic that has been championed by the liberals of our day to twist the Scriptures to teach that jesus was not born of the virgin Mary, that propitiation by the substitutionary atonement of our Lord Jesus Christ is a barbaric relic of primitive man’s thinking, and that the bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ is mythical. Other casualties of this hermeneutic include: Moses being the human author of the Pentateuch, the historic i ty of the book of jonah (his being swallowed by a big fish and being in its belly three days and nights), the crossing of the Red Sea rather than the reed sea, the historic i ty of the ten plagues, etc. Whereas, Westminster Presbytery does declare and make known to the world and to all churches, especially our own denomination, our churches, our presbyteries, our General Assembly and the seminaries from which our candidates arise, that we will not tolerate these views in any teaching elder seeking admittance to this Presbytery, or any other man seeking to be licensed or to become a candidate for the ministry under care of this Presbytery. Furthermore, Westminster Presbytery considers that any view which departs from the confessional doctrine of creation in six 24 hour days strikes at the fundamentals of the system of doctrine set forth in the Holy Scriptures. Therefore be it resolved that the 26th General Assembly of the PCA appoint a study committee, comprised of 4 Teaching Elders and 3 Ruling Elders from 7 different presbyteries fora period of one year, to study the issue of Creation and to bring to the 27* General Assembly a proposed statement of the PCA’s beliefs concerning this issue. This Committee would be funded from the Administrative Committee budget up to $ 8, 000 . 4 That the Committee advise the Stated Clerk that Communication 4 from Westminster Presbytery and Communication 10 from Potomac Presbytery be VACATED on the grounds that they do not conform to RAO 10-1,2. Adopted 5. That OVERTURE 1 from Potomac Presbytery be answered in the affirmative with the following substitution (see also Committee on Constitutional Business report, p. 228). Adopted and sent down to presbyteries for advice and consent

“Amend BCO 13-5 to Clarify Membership of One Honorably Retired” [Should be entitled “to clarify membership of a teaching elder without call Who Needs to Relocate”] Whereas, the requirement of BCO 13-2, “A minister shall be required to hold his membership in the Presbytery within whose geographical bounds he resides...” appears in some cases to be in tension with the direction offered in BCO 13-5, “Ordinarily, only a minister who receives a call to a definite ecclesiastical work within the bound sofa particular presbytery may be received as a member of that Presbytery except in cases where the minister is already honorably retired, or in those cases deemed necessary by the Presbytery ”; Therefore, Potomac Presbytery overtures the Twenty-Sixth General Assembly to amend the Book of Church Order 13-5 by adding a new sentence after the words ‘review of the General Assembly.’, as follows: 'In such cases deemed necessary, which may include the case of a minister without call whose circumstances appear to require relocation within the bounds of that Presbytery, the time allotment of BCO 13-2 shall be counted from the day the minister was first continued on the roll without call in any Presbytery. ’ So that the amended paragraph reads, 13-5 ‘Ordinarily, only a minister who receives a call to a definite ecclesiastical work within the bounds of a particular Presbytery may be received as a member of that Presbytery except in cases where the minister is already honorably retired, or in those cases deemed necessary by the Presbytery, subject to the review of the General Assembly. In such cases deemed necessary, which may include the case of a minister without call whose circumstances appear to require relocation within the bounds of that Presbytery, the time allotment of BCO 13-2 shall be counted from the day the minister was first continued on the roll without call in any Presbytery’’ [Note: material in italics is the proposed new language in the BCO.] 6. That Overture 14 from SE Louisiana Presbytery be answered by reference to the General Assembly’s action on Overture 1 (see also item 5, above, and Committee on Constitutional Business, p. 229). Adopted

“Amend BCO 41 to Clarify Ministerial Service Out of Bounds” Whereas, The Book of Church Order of the Presbyterian Church in America, chapter 46-1, requires the teaching and ruling elders of the congregation to maintain oversight of a member who has moved beyond the bounds of the local church, as far as possible, and Whereas, the same chapter requires the teaching and ruling elders of the congregation to notify the teaching and ruling elders of a congregation within whose bounds that member has moved, in order that said member be encouraged to transfer his membership, and Whereas, this is done for the spiritual benefit of such a member who has moved beyond the bounds of his local congregation, and Whereas, there are many teaching elders, whose membership is help by the Presbytery rather than the local congregation, who are without call and who have been forced by the requirements of supporting their families to move beyond the geographical bounds of the Presbytery holding their membership, and Whereas, there is no provision in the Book of Church Order for any Presbytery to receive or take oversight of a teaching elder who is without a call, but who resides within the bounds of said Presbytery, and it is impossible for a Presbytery to provide adequate oversight or counsel from a great distance, and Whereas, it would seem obvious that a teaching elder in such a situation would be in, at least, as great a need of spiritual oversight and support as any other member of the church. Therefore, we request that a provision be added to the Book of Church Order which would require a teaching elder, without a call, who has cause to move outside the geographical bounds of the Presbytery which holds his membership, to request the Presbytery into whose bounds he has moved, to receive him as an associate member of Presbytery, under similar conditions to the Book of Church Order provisions for associate members of a congregation in chapter 46-4. Such associate members of Presbytery shall be examined by the receiving Presbytery as to their views, shall be permitted to fill the pulpits within the Presbytery upon request, and can serve on committees at the discretion of Presbytery, but may not hold office or chair a committee, nor shall he have the right to vote in the Presbytery until such time as he shall receive a call and become a full member of Presbytery. Presbytery shall provide such oversight, care, and counsel as needful until such time as the associate member shall accept another call and be examined and received by the Presbytery within whose bounds such a call originated, or until divestiture from the ministry takes place. Such divestiture should be accomplished by the Presbytery of which said teaching elder is a full member, and can be done either at the instigation of the Presbytery of last full membership, or by request to that Presbytery from the one holding associate membership, or at the request of the teaching elder. This provision will eliminate the sad experience of those teaching elders who are without call and far removed from the bounds of the Presbytery holding their membership, requiring them to be out of fellowship through no fault of their own. 7. That Overture 2 from Potomac Presbytery be answered in the affirmative with the editorial corrections noted (see also Committee on Constitutional Business, p. 229). Adopted and sent down to presbyteries for advice and consent

"Amend BCO 20-2 to Clarify Role of Pastor Search Committee" Whereas, the Book of Church Order does not specify the duties of a pastoral search committee appointed by the congregation; Whereas, in newly planted churches where members may not be fully acquainted with Presbyterian practices and procedures such a lack of specification can and has led to confusion among some of our churches; and Whereas, the Twenty-Fifth General Assembly remanded an overture from Potomac Presbytery for refinement, which work is now accomplished. Therefore, Potomac Presbytery overtures the Twenty-Sixth General Assembly to amend the Book of Church Order 20-2 by adding a new concluding sentence to the second paragraph, after the words "as designated by the congregation (see BCO 25).", as follows: "The pulpit committee shall, after consultation and deliberation, recommend to the congregation a pastoral candidate who, in its judgment, fulfills the Constitutional requirements of that office (e.g., BCO 8, 13-6 and 21) and is most suited to be profitable to the spiritual interests of the congregation (cf. *BCO* 20-6).” 8. That Overture 4 from Potomac Presbytery be answered in the affirmative as amended. *Adopted*

“Amend *BCO* 13-12 to Clarify Circumstances for a Special Meeting of Presbytery” Whereas, the Book of Church Order appears to require an emergency for the calling of a special meeting of a Presbytery (13-12. . . When any emergency shall require a meeting earlier than the time to which the Presbytery stands adjourned, the Moderator shall . . . call a special meeting. . .); and Whereas, the word *emergency* is defined as “a sudden, generally unexpected occurrence or set of circumstances demanding immediate action” (*Webster’s New World Dictionary*, 3rd ed. (1994), s.v.); Whereas, there are circumstances with respect to which a special meeting of Presbytery might be convenient, but which could not fairly be called an emergency (e.g., to hear the report of a study committee or a special commission, to examine and receive ministers transferring into the Presbytery, etc.); Therefore, Potomac Presbytery overtures the Twenty-sixth General Assembly to amend the Book of Church Order 13-12 by replacing the second sentences of *BCO* 13-12 with the following: > The Moderator shall call a special meeting at the request or with the concurrence of two Teaching Elders and two Ruling Elders from at least three different churches. 9. That Overture 12 from the Session of Bedford Presbyterian Church be answered in the negative. *Adopted* **Grounds:** The Overture appears to misunderstand the nature of the “rule” referred to in *BCO* 7-2. In our judgment “rule” refers, not to any exercise of authority in the church, but to the overall exercise of government in the church belonging exclusively to the eldership. Clearly some measure of authority (and therefore corresponding obedience on the part of the people) is required in the deacon’s calling to administer and direct the congregation’s efforts in service (cf. Acts 6; I Tim. 3:12; *BCO* 9-2). The current vow is well-adapted to accommodate this truth, in that it requires that obedience “to which *his office*, according to the Word of God and the Constitution of this church, entitles him.” (emphasis added).

source: OVERTURE 12 From the Session of Bedford Presbyterian Church
body: “Amend BCO 24-5 RE Congregational Vows respecting Deacons” Whereas, BCO 7-2 rightly declares “The office of deacon is not one of rule, but rather of service both to the physical and spiritual needs of the people,” and Whereas, this means that it is inappropriate to call the congregation to give obedience to the deacons, Therefore the Session of Bedford Presbyterian Church overtures the 26th General Assembly to add in the question to the congregation in BCO 24-5, after “obedience”, (for deacons substitute ‘and encouragement’ for ‘encouragement and obedience’)”. REASON: the PCA is a presbyterian and not a baptist denomination. Forwarded from the Session of Bedford Presbyterian Church, without the concurrence of presbytery. 10. “Amend BCO 32-6 To Clarify Provisions for Contumacy” Whereas, the honor of Christ and His church are damaged by persons who assail the rules to flout the court; and Whereas, BCO 32-6 is vague, in that the provisions for contumacy are never clearly “hereinafter provided;” and Whereas, the framers of the BCO intended that contumacy should be dealt with in a timely, and expeditious manner; Therefore, be it resolved that the session of the rock presbyterian church overtures the twenty-sixth General Assembly to change the Book of Church Order 32-6 from its present reading: “if he appear and refuse to plead he shall be dealt with for his contumacy, as hereinafter provided.” To read instead: “if he appear and refuse to plead, or flout the court and/or otherwise reject its authority, he shall be dealt with for his contumacy immediately.” 11. That Overture 20 from Ascension Presbytery be answered in the negative. Adopted Grounds: The General Assembly has provided adequate guidance on this issue in the “Response to ‘Evangelicals and Catholics Together’” which was adopted by the 23rd General Assembly. (M23GA , pp. 229-231.)

source: OVERTURE 20 From the Presbytery of the Ascension
body: “Declare the Roman Catholic Church to be Apostate” Whereas, the Roman Catholic Church (RCC) does not found itself upon the 66 books of the Bible as its only source of authority but also upon additional books, RCC tradition, and upon papal authority; and Whereas, the RCC does not teach that salvation is strictly by grace alone through faith alone in Jesus Christ alone, and Whereas, there are many errors taught, which result logically from the foregoing statements, therefore be it resolved that the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America (PCA) declares that the Roman Catholic Church is not a true Biblical Christian church, and Be it further resolved that the PCA calls upon all members of the RCC who profess the true biblical Christian faith to come out of the RCC and join the PCA or some other similar biblical church. 12. That Overture 21 from the Presbytery of the Ascension be answered in the negative (see also Committee on Constitutional Business, p. 230). Adopted Grounds: The material in the proposed vow is already accounted for in the 4th vow (“Do you promise to support the Church in its worship and work to the best of your ability?”). The work of the church is nothing other than to glorify Christ in the gathering, perfecting, and preserving God’s elect, through the ministry of word and sacrament, by the power of the Spirit. the worship of the church is nothing other than devotion to our triune God in private, in our families, and in public, using the means God has appointed in His Word. To promise to support the church in this calling is precisely to “promise to make diligent use of all the means of grace which Christ, through His Church, has provided ”

source: OVERTURE 21 From the Presbytery of the Ascension
body: “Amend BCO 57-5 by adding New Question for Members” Whereas, many in our churches neglect to avail themselves of opportunities to grow in our Lord Jesus Christ, Whereas, many fail to make Sunday School, Bible studies, special classes, etc. a high priority on their schedules, Whereas, many have not created a heritage for their children of family bible study, devotions, and worship in their homes, Whereas, Paul’s admonition to Timothy to “Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, handling accurately the word of truth.” (2 Timothy 2:15) is applicable to all of us, laity as well as pastors, Whereas, inclusion of the suggested question below would provide added opportunity for leaders to explain to those joining the church, their responsibilities and privileges with respect to the various means of grace available through the ministry of the church and home, Be it resolved to add to the questions in BCO 57-5, a question which in substance used to appear in the old presbyterian Book of Church Order - namely “Do you promise to make diligent use of all the means of grace which Christ, through His Church, has provided?” It is suggested that this question be numbered question 5, and the current Question 5 be renumbered as Question 6. 13 That Overture 24 from the Session of New Life Presbyterian Church be answered in the negative (see also Committee on Constitutional Business, p 230). Adopted Grounds: See the rationale adopted by the 21st General Assembly set forth below: a. In recognition that this is the "Lord's table," 1 Corinthians 10:21, not the table of one church only, BCO 58-4 permits "open communion," that is, allowing members in good standing of any evangelical church to partake, and "close communion," which permits only those members of other churches who have been examined and approved by the Session to partake (It does not permit "closed communion," the practice of excluding all but members of the particular congregation). b. In the judgment of charity, we believe that other evangelical churches have examined and found credible the faith of their members and, on the basis of this presumed approval, in "open communion" we invite members of other churches to the Lord's table in our midst. In "close communion," the Session of a particular church itself determines the credibility of a visitor's profession of faith. There is no such available assessment in this life for members of the Invisible Church. c. Baptism is into a community of believers, that is a church. Unbaptized people certainly should not be permitted to come to the Table. Of course unbaptized people credibly professing faith in Christ and seeking admittance to the Table should be baptized with all proper speed, and thereupon admitted to the Table. At this point, these communicants are baptized members of a visible church. d. One cannot love Christ and eschew His bride. The credible profession of persons unwilling to unite to Christ's Church must be questioned. Any sinful unwillingness to unite with Christ's people should be addressed pastorally (Hebrews 10:25; 1 Corinthians 10:16-17). Those unwilling to unite to Christ's Church are outside the visible body of Christ. e. One cannot be subject to Christ and not be subject to the government He has appointed in His Church. Believers become subject to the government of the Church through their covenantal vows of membership (Ephesians 4:11-12; Hebrews 13:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13). f. Church discipline is necessary for properly maintaining the Lord's Table; such discipline is unavailable apart from membership in a visible church. g. This overture implies that there is no biblical ground for the keeping of a roll of members of the visible church, and therefore of people who may partake of the church's sacrament. However, the clear evidence of Scripture is that the church should keep a roll of members. The supreme model for our membership roll is the membership roll of heaven (Exodus 32:32,33; Daniel 12:1; Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 13:8; 20:12,15). The Biblical pattern is for new believers to be "numbered" or "added to" the rolls of the local church (Acts 2:41,47; 6:7; 1 Timothy 5:9). Members could be taken away from the roll (1 Corinthians 5:2)-this indicates more than being physically barred, since even unbelievers could attend Christian worship (1 Corinthians 14:23)-or reinstated (2 Corinthians 2:6-7); it is impossible to have coherent discipline without such a roll. There was a widow's roll for diaconal purposes (1 Timothy 5:9). Elders are to know their sheep, and are accountable for the care of the flock entrusted to them-this demands knowing who they are; that is, it demands a list or roll (Hebrews 13:7,17-19; 1 Thessalonians 5:11-14; 1 Peter 5:2; Acts 20:28). The apostolic church utilized letters of transfer or commendation (Acts 18:27; Romans 16:1-2; 2 Corinthians 3:1; 8:23-24); examples of these letters include Philemon and 3 John. Interchurch business was conducted by people with reference letters (1 Corinthians 16:3; 2 Corinthians 8:16-24). We conclude therefore that requiring professed believers to be enrolled as members of an evangelical church as a condition for taking the Lord's Supper is consistent with sound Biblical practice. (M2IGA pp. 141-142)

source: OVERTURE 24 From New Life Presbyterian Church
body: “Amend BCO 58-4 to Clarify the Fencing of the Lord’s Table” Whereas, the Scriptures teach that the Lord’s Supper is open to those who profess true faith in the Person and work of Jesus Christ alone for the forgiveness of their sins; and Whereas, there is confusion among numerous churches concerning the meaning of BCO 58-4, resulting in a significant number of our churches practicing a “face value” reading and application of the last paragraph of BCO 58-4; and Whereas, the historic interpretation of the language of BCO 58-4 goes beyond the requirements of both the Scriptures and the Westminster Standards concerning admission to the Lord’s Table; and Whereas, there are certain rare and extraordinary cases where a Session would be prudent in fencing the Lord’s Table to admit profession believers who at the time of the celebration are not on the membership roll of an evangelical church. Therefore we recommend that the third paragraph of BCO 58-4 be revised as follows: **Current BCO 58-4**: Since, by our Lord’s appointment, this Sacrament sets forth the Communion of the Saints, the minister, at the discretion of the Session, before the observance begins, may either invite all those who profess the true religion, and are communicants in good standing in any evangelical church, to participate in the ordinance; or may invite those who have been approved by the Session, after having given indication of their desire to participate. It is proper also to give a special invitation to non-communicants to remain during the service. **Proposed Change**: Since, by our Lord’s appointment, this Sacrament sets forth the Communion of the Saints, the minister, at the discretion of the Session, before the observance begins, may either invite: (1) all those who profess the true religion, and are communicants in good standing in any evangelical church to participate in the ordinance; or may invite those (2) the communicant members of this church, and those communing members of other churches who have been approved by the Session, after having given indication of their desire to participate. In addition, the minister may invite those who profess the true religion and are baptized, but due to extraordinary circumstances acceptable to the Session are not currently on the roll of any evangelical church, who have been approved by the Session after having given indication of their desire to participate. It is also proper to give a special invitation to non-communicants to remain during the service. 14. That Overture 25 from Central Carolina Presbytery be answered in the affirmative with the following substitution (see also Committee on Constitutional Business, p. 230) Adopted as amended and sent down to presbyteries for advice and consent

“Amend BCO 24-1 to Close Nominations One Month Prior to Congregational Meeting” Whereas, BCO 24-1 requires public notice of the time, place and purpose at least one month prior to the appointed time of electing officers, during which time the congregation is asked to submit names to the Session; and Whereas, BCO 24-1 requires the Session to examine those nominated and then report to the congregation before election day those eligible for election, and Whereas, these two requirements can place undue time constraints upon the Session to examine candidates and report to the congregation before the election day, Therefore, the session of prosperity church petitions the General Assembly through Central Carolina Presbytery to amend BCO 24-1 by substituting the following for BCO 24-1 [Note: material in italics is new material in the BCO]: A. Substitute the following for the first paragraph: 24-1. Every church shall elect persons to the officers of ruling elder and deacon in the following manner: At such times as determined by the Session, communicant members of the congregation may submit names to the Session, keeping in mind that each prospective officer shall be an active male member who meets the qualifications set forth in I Timothy 3 and Titus 1. After the close of the nomination period nominees for the office of riding elder and/or deacon shall receive instruction in the qualifications and work of the office. Each nominee shall then be examined in B. Substitute for second paragraph (i.e., “The Session shall examine. . .”) the following: If there are candidates eligible for election, the Session shall report to the congregation those eligible, giving at least 30 days prior notice of the time and place of a congregational meetingfor elections. Grounds: BCO 24-1 requires public notice of the time, place and purpose at least one month prior to the appointed time of electing officers, during which time the congregation is asked to submit names to the Session. BCO 24-1 requires the Session to examine those nominated and then report to the congregation before election day those eligible for election. These two requirements can place undue time constraints upon the Session to examine candidates and report to the congregation before the election day.

“Erect an ad interim committee to study the role of women in Combat” Whereas, God, the creator of male and female (Genesis 1, 2, is the Author of their distinctive roles (Gen. 2, 1 Cor. 11), as well as the distinctive afflictions they face in light of man’s fall into sin (Gen. 3); and Whereas, war is the result of fallen man’s sinfulness (Gen. 4; James 4:1-2), and thus affects men, women, and children with its horror and devastation (Jos. 6:20-21; 2 Kings 25); and Whereas, the Church which is to be salt and light (Matt. 5) is to proclaim the Good News that God is reconciling men, women, and children to Himself in Christ, not counting their sins against them (2 Cor. 5:19), and to speak clearly to the world as to how we are to live both personally and as a society (Psa. 119:46, 138:4, Acts 9:15), and Whereas, men are called by God in Scripture to protect their daughters and wives not only as fathers and husbands (Num. 30:1-16), Ruth 2 & 3, 1 Cor. 11, Eph. 5) but also as military combatants (Deut. 20; Jos 6:20-21; Psa 144:1), and Whereas, governing officials of both church and state are instituted by god as His ministers and therefore are accountable to God by the light of nature and as His will is expressed in Holy Scripture (Rom 13; 1 Cor 4, 1 Tim 3); and Whereas, our American government has implemented an unwise military policy of deploying men and women together in intimate quarters for military combat and immediate engagement with hostile lethal force; and Whereas, Christians are forbidden by the sixth commandment from “all taking away the life of ourselves, or of others, except in case of public justice, lawful war, or necessary defense,” ( WLC, Q 136:1-5); and Whereas, some PCA Sessions have begun to counsel their women that service in combat roles is morally wrong (January 1998 Minutes, Presbytery of Philadelphia), I. THEREFORE BE IT NOW RESOLVED, that the 26th General Assembly of the PCA reaffirm its moral commitment to the following truths of God’s eternal and unchangeable Law: 1. That “the honor that inferiors owe to their superiors ‘includes’ defense, and maintenance of their persons and authority, according to their several ranks, and the nature of their places;” (WLC, Q. 127:30,31)’ 2. That it “is required of superiors toward their inferiors” to provide for the “protecting, and providing for them all things necessary for soul and body;” (WLC, Q. 129:54-56), 3. That “the sins of superiors” include “commanding things unlawful, or not in the power of inferiors to perform; counseling, encouraging, or favoring them in that which is evil; dissuading, discouraging, or discountenancing them in that which is good, careless exposing, or leaving them to wrong, temptation, and danger,” (WLC, Q 130:64-69, 71), 4 That the “duties required in the sixth commandment” include “avoiding all occasions, temptations, and practices, which tend to the unjust taking away the life of any, by just defense thereof against violence,” (WLC, Q. 135:89-92), 5. That the “duties required in the seventh commandment are, chastity in body, mind, affections, words, and behavior, and the preservation of it in ourselves and others,” (WLC, Q. 137:22-25); 6. That the seventh commandment also requires “marriage by those that have not the gift of continency, conjugal love, and cohabitation,... shunning all occasions of uncleanness, and resisting temptations thereunto.” ( WLC,Q 138:30-34), and 7, That the sins forbidden in the seventh commandment include “unchaste company; .. and all other provocations to, or actions of uncleanness, either in ourselves or others ” ( WLC, Q. 139:52, 54). II. AND MAY IT BE FURTHER RESOLVED, that the 26th General Assembly of the PCA establish a six-person committee composed of two representatives elected from and by the Philadelphia Presbytery, Chaplain Stephen W Leonard, and two others elected by the 26th General Assembly, as well as a national leader of the PCA Women In the Church to serve as an additional nonvoting consultant, to report back to the 27th General Assembly of the PCA with answers to the following questions along with their recommendations: 1 Does the right and duty that women have to self-“defense” that may involve physical violence in a time of “just war” (e.g. Jud. 9:53) justify women’s service in immediate combat roles and/or military service? 2. Does the intimate “cohabitation “ of men and women required by combatants in the current army and navy violate: A The principle of “cohabitation” for only marriage? B The duty to avoid “unchaste company. . and all other provocations to, or acts of uncleanness, either in ourselves or others”? C. The duty of superiors to inferiors to “provide for them all things necessary for soul and body?” 3. Do the intimate conditions required by current army and navy policy constitute any of the following: A A “careless exposing” of inferiors by superiors to “wrong, temptation and danger?” BAn impediment to perform the duty to have “chastity in body, mind, affections, words, and behavior; and the preservation of it in ourselves and others9” C. An impediment to perform the duty of “shunning all occasions of uncleanness, and resisting temptations thereunto”? 4. Inasmuch as the Scriptures declare that husbands are to honor their wives as the “weaker partners” (1 Peter 3:7), does the placing of women in combat conditions and/or military service: A Constitute “commanding” what is “unlawful”, or “not in the power of inferiors to perform9” B Constitute a breach of the duty of superiors toward their inferiors to provide for their “protecting,” and “providing for them all things necessary for soul and body” {WLC, Q. 129:54-56)? 5. May a Christian woman refuse to be drafted for military service for a “just war” on conscientious grounds (should such an eventuality arise as is predicted by all involved in the current debate)? May this be done by appeal to the Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 135 - “the duties required in the sixth commandment are the avoiding all occasions, temptations, and practices, which tend to the unjust taking away the life of any, by just defense thereof against violence,” since the potential of women dying in combat is an “unjust taking away the life of any” a swell as not a “just defense”? 6. Does the PCA’s provision of chaplains to the military in spite of its current policies on women in combat roles and/or military service constitute the sin of superiors toward inferiors of “counseling, encouraging, or favoring them in that which is evil”? 7. Is the PCA’s current silence on the issue of women in combat roles tantamount to the sins of superiors against inferiors by “dissuading, discouraging, or discountenancing them in that which is good”9 8 Should the conclusion be reached that the current military policy regarding women in combat roles and/or military service is not only unwise but morally wrong, should the church be satisfied to exercise its general discipline against its members who teach or practice women in combat roles, or should it seek to institute judicial process against such (BCO 27:1)? 9. Any other relevant questions that come before the committee III. AND MAY IT BE FINALLY RESOLVED: 1 That the 26th General Assembly urge our male and female members who are considering or presently engaged in military service to take counsel of their sessions as to the teaching of God’s Word in the matter of the role of men and women in military combat roles, also referring them to the Minutes of the Twenty-Fifth General Assembly, pp, 185ff, 2. That the Stated Clerk of the General Assembly send a copy of this overture to the North American Presbyterian and Reformed Council (NAPARC), to the national associations of evangelicals (NAE), and to our military chaplains, asking them for their advice and concerns on these matters, 3. That the Stated Clerk of the General Assembly send a letter to those governmental and military officials and military chaplains who are currently in the policy debates regarding the relationship of men and women in combat roles, expressing the PCA’s commitment to the unchanging moral law of God as expressed through our Larger Catechism as cited above in Resolution 1.1-7. This letter shall urge them to honor God’s law in their policy decision, and shall further inform them that the PCA is discussing this matter and intends to provide further moral guidance in subsequent Assembly decisions. 4. That the PCA’s Committee for Christian Education and Publications, in consultation with the Women In the Church and the PCA’s chaplains, develop guidelines and instructional materials that will encourage and equip military personnel for growth in spiritual holiness in the context of current military policy on men and women in combat roles.
