source: OVERTURE 15 From Central Carolina Presbytery (to CCB & B&O)
body: “Amend BCO 35-7 and 32-18 Requiring Recording of Testimony and Provision for Transcription” This overture would substitute new language for BCO 35-7, and strike one word from BCO 32-18. Chapter 35 - Evidence 35-7. Every question put to a witness shall, if required, be reduced to writing. When answered, it shall, together with the answer, be recorded, if deemed by the court or by either party of sufficient importance, and the testimony of the witness shall be read to him for his approbation and subscription. Proposed new 35-7 All testimony shall be recorded (transcription, audiotape, videotape, or some other electronic means) and witnesses informed of such prior to testifying. Such recording becomes part of the Record of the Case. However, in order to be referenced in written or oral briefs, such recording must be transcribed and the transcription authenticated by the trial court. The court of final appeal may assess the cost of transcription equitably among the parties. Chapter 32 – General Provisions Applicable to all Cases of Process 32-18 Minutes of the trial shall be kept by the clerk, which shall exhibit the charges, the answer, written record of the testimony, as defined by BCO 35-7, and all such acts, orders, and decisions of the court relating to the case, as either party may desire, and also the judgment... Rationale – The current wording of *BCO 35-7* does not ensure a complete record of all the testimony in a trial. Therefore, if an appeal or a complaint is filed, there may not be a sufficient record of the testimony. This change would ensure that a complete record of testimony is available. This recording provision is similar to that in SJC Manual 19.2: “All oral arguments by the parties before the Commission or a Judicial Panel thereof shall be tape recorded.” Furthermore, the current language of 35-7 is unclear and cumbersome. What is meant by “if required” in the first sentence? Who determines if it is required? The second sentence implies that only some of the testimony might be recorded. Nowadays, since electronic means are easily available for recording, there is no reason not to record all the testimony. If *BCO 35-7* is changed as above, the word “written” needs to be stricken from *BCO 32-18*. The recorded testimony would be considered part of the minutes, regardless of the form of the recording. Adopted at the Winter Stated Meeting of Central Carolina Presbytery on January 26, 2001. Attested by: /s/ David Frierson, Stated Clerk 13. Answer Overture 17 from Central Carolina Presbytery (“Add a New Chapter 44 to *BCO* and Appendix H”) in the affirmative, with amendment, by appending the proposed language with suitable amendments and the flowchart to the *BCO* as Appendix H – “Suggested Procedures for Presbytery Judicial Commissions Acting as Appellate Courts.” Grounds: 1) The overture is intended to offer assistance in cases in which commissions act as appellate courts. To make this procedural advice available quickly, it was deemed wise to avoid the amendment procedure. 2) We believe this extensive procedure best serves the Church by being placed in the Appendix, where it is non-binding. Adopted Appendix H Suggested Procedures for Presbytery Judicial Commissions Acting as Appellate Courts 1. These procedures are suggested when a Presbytery, as an appellate court, decides that an appeal or complaint arising from a Session is in order, and in accordance with *BCO* 15, chooses to appoint a Judicial Commission to hear the case. The Presbytery Stated Clerk shall promptly notify the parties of the names of the Commission members and the initial contact information. (See flowchart.) 2. A hearing shall not be conducted until the Commission determines that the Record of the Case is complete (perfected), the parties have had opportunity to file briefs, and the members of the Commission have had adequate time to read the Record and all briefs. 3. The convener or chairman of the Commission shall convene the first meeting within 10 days of the Presbytery meeting at which the Commission was appointed. This meeting may be held the same day Presbytery appoints the Commission. At this convening meeting the Commission shall elect its chairman and secretary, unless Presbytery had previously appointed them. In addition to other preliminary matters, the Commission may discuss potential dates for a hearing and the current status of the Record. The chairman shall promptly notify the parties of all addresses necessary for filing purposes. 4. Conference calls are acceptable for all Commission meetings other than the hearing. This includes the meetings to: 1) convene the Commission, 2) resolve disputes on the Record, 3) adopt a Judgment, and 4) adopt a written decision and approve minutes. 5. At its discretion and with the consent of both parties, the Commission may decide to accept email, fax or similar means for filings after establishing procedures to confirm the date that a document is filed and received. 6. Record of the Case – After the Commission is appointed, the Presbytery Stated Clerk shall promptly ensure delivery of the Record to each Commission member and to all parties to the case. It shall be delivered to the appellant/complainant in person or in some other manner providing verification of the date of receipt. If the appellant/complainant believes the Record is incomplete or incorrect, he shall, within 14 days of receiving such Record, file written notice with the Commission and with the Session (clerk or respondent). Such notice shall specify the alleged defects and suggestions for corrections. Failure to file a timely objection will constitute acceptance of the Record. Within 14 days of receiving such written notice, the Session shall file a written response with the Commission and with the appellant/complainant. The chairman shall promptly send to the commissioners the notice of objection and the Session’s response. If no objection is filed, the parties are considered to have …

“Ask CCB to Examine Minutes of SJC regarding Original Jurisdiction in John Wood Judicial Matter” Whereas, the 28th General Assembly voted to take jurisdiction of Dr. John Wood with respect to allegations set forth in overtures from three presbyteries; and Whereas, the matter was referred to the SJC to be considered “after the manner of BCO 31-2;” and Whereas, the 28th General Assembly directed that, as part of this process, “representatives from the petitioning presbyteries be permitted to represent their allegations before the SJC” (M28GA, p. 310); and Whereas, Presbytery received, from the Investigative Panel appointed by the SJC, a letter stating that the Panel would be meeting “...for the sole purpose of gathering information...” and asking that we identify witnesses “...who have direct knowledge of relevant facts...;” and Whereas, Presbytery understood “represent their allegations” to entail, not just a right to identify witnesses, but also a right to explain our reasoning and concerns; and Whereas, the contents of the Panel’s letter indicated to us that there would not be an opportunity for us to “represent our allegations” before the Panel in the way in which the 28th General Assembly meant that phrase; and Whereas, we sent a letter to the Panel detailing this and other concerns, and asking for a fuller explanation of the SJC’s planned process, particularly as it related to “permitting us to represent our allegations;” and Whereas, Presbytery never received a formal response to its letter; and Whereas, in a telephone call, initiated by the Stated Clerk of Presbytery, the Secretary of the Panel stated that it was his understanding that representatives from the Presbytery of the Ascension would not be allowed to speak before the Investigative Panel on the grounds that they had no ability to testify from direct knowledge regarding the facts of the case; and Whereas, on the basis of the above letter and conversation, Presbytery’s Commission determined that it would not be good stewardship to send a representative to the Panel’s meeting if he would not be able to speak to Presbytery’s position (and having no information as to whether we would be permitted to address the full SJC); and Whereas, it is our understanding that the two men from the other petitioning presbyteries (one of whom was an elected representative of his presbytery) were allowed to speak to the Panel only with regard to their knowledge of facts, and not with regard to a presentation of the allegations; and Whereas, no one from this Presbytery received any notification or permission to attend the meeting of the full SJC, much less to “represent any allegations;” and Whereas, to the best of our knowledge, neither of the other two petitioning presbyteries received such an invitation; and Whereas, the above facts seem to indicate that the Standing Judicial Commission acted in direct violation of the instructions of the 28th General Assembly; and Whereas, the current Standing Judicial Commission is clearly a commission of the 28th GA (see M28GA, p. 245); and Whereas, commissions, by their very nature, must operate within the procedures and guidelines mandated by the body appointing them lest their power be unchecked; and Whereas, this is particularly true in this matter which was assigned to the SJC by the General Assembly, and which does not fall into any of the categories mentioned in the RAO and SJC Manual as being under the ordinary purview of the SJC [i.e., appeals, complaints, and judicial references (see RAO 15-1 and SJC Manual sec. 13-15)]; and Whereas, RAO 15-1 and SJC Manual 20.5 charge the Committee on Constitutional Business with reviewing the minutes of the SJC to determine if the SJC has conformed to the requirements of the RAO and Manual; and Whereas, if the SJC failed to carry out the instructions of the 28th General Assembly it has failed to act properly as a commission, thus violating the BCO and RAO; and Whereas, this overture raises questions only about the procedures followed by the SJC, not its reasoning; Therefore Be it Resolved, that the Presbytery of the Ascension hereby overtures the 29th General Assembly, through its Committee on Constitutional Business, asking that the CCB examine the minutes of the Standing Judicial Commission to determine if the instructions of the 28th General Assembly were followed with regard to the matter of permitting representatives of the petitioning presbyteries to “represent their allegations before the SJC;” and, it not, to take or recommend appropriate action as per RAO 15-1, para. 4 (cf. BCO 40-4, last sentence). Adopted at the January Stated Meeting of the Presbytery of the Ascension on January 27, 2001. Attested by: /s/ Frederick R. Neikirk, Stated Clerk 15. That Overture 21 from Ellisville Presbyterian Church (“Amend BCO 13-1 to Allow at Least Two Ruling Elders to Represent Each Congregation in Presbytery Meetings”) be answered in the affirmative. Adopted

source: OVERTURE 21 From Ellisville Presbyterian Church (to B&O & CCB)
body: “Amend BCO 13-1 to Allow at Least Two Ruling Elders to Represent Each Congregation in Presbytery Meetings” Whereas, the formation of the Presbyterian Church in America was the result of the Lord, in His Providence, convicting elders of the need to remain true to the Biblical principles and teachings upon which our faith is based, and Whereas, our elder fathers in the faith were the first to point out and take a stand against errors being made and taught in the old Southern church, and Whereas, John Edward Richard, in his History of the Presbyterian Church in America (1986, p. 131) posits, “There seems to be a desire in the pre-birth movement of the new church to give right concern and positions to all officers, whether lay or ministerial. We may even hope to return to decentralized polity so wisely advocated by James H. Thornwell near the birth of the Southern church,” and Whereas, the Scriptures of the Old Testament in 1 Kings 12:1-5, 18, which record King Rehoboam’s fateful rejecting and discarding of the wisdom of “the elders (who) had stood before his father Solomon while he still lived” and how Rehoboam instead consulted and followed only the advice of “the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him,” clearly demonstrate the tragic results of rejecting and discarding the wisdom of old and wise elders, and Whereas, the Scriptures of the New Testament in 1 Timothy 3:1-7, especially require that the elder be a man who “is not a novice” plainly declaring the desirability and advantage of those elders who are men not only of demonstrable godliness but of rich and lengthy experience in walking with the Lord, that they may wisely serve in the courts of the church, and Whereas, ruling elders have played an integral part in the organization and growth of the Presbyterian Church in America, serving diligently in all courts of the church, and Whereas, the parity of the eldership is compromised when the composition of church courts contain substantially more teaching elder commissioners than ruling elder commissioners, and Whereas, in 1999, 2873 teaching elders held membership in the 58 presbyteries numbering 1206 churches (Minutes, 28th General Assembly), and Whereas, in presbytery meetings, 2873 teaching elders might dominate the business of the church brought from the Sessions of the 1206 churches, and could exert clergical [sic] influence at the presbytery court level that may disregard the needs of grass roots Session courts, and Whereas, Proverbs 11:14 and 24:6 make it clear that the more counsel (wisdom) brought to the issues before the church, the greater the probability the building of the kingdom will be achieved, and Whereas, the more participation by ruling elders at the lower court levels (Session and Presbytery), the greater will be the probability that there will be interest in and counsel provided by ruling elders on the issues and problems that confront the churches at the grass roots level of the denomination, and Whereas, ruling elders serve the church generally, when called thereunto (BCO 8-3; Acts 20:28f), as well as the local congregation, and Whereas, the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America early recognized the need for more ruling elder involvement and participation in said Court by amending the Book of Church Order so as to increase the number of ruling elder commissioners from each church from one (1) to two (2), with additional commissioners for larger congregations; and Whereas, there is a similar need for more ruling elder involvement and participation in the church presbytery court, Now therefore Be it Resolved that the undersigned Session overtures the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America to amend to Book of Church Order, 13-1, to increase the number of ruling elder commissioners to presbytery meetings from each church from one (1) to two (2), with additional commissioners for larger congregations, and Be It Further Resolved, that the Book of Church Order 13-1 be amended by deleting the present paragraphs and substituting the following, to wit: The Presbytery consists of all the teaching elders and churches within its bounds that have been accepted by the Presbytery. When the Presbytery meets as a court it shall comprise all teaching elders and ruling elders as elected by their Session. Each congregation is entitled to two (2) ruling elder representatives for the first 350 communing members or fraction thereof, and one additional ruling elder for each additional 500 communing members or fraction thereof. Adopted by the Session at a stated meeting on the 12th day of November, 2000. Attested by: /s/ Charlie H. Probst, Clerk of Session of Ellisville Presbyterian Church This overture was submitted at the 90th Stated Meeting of Grace Presbytery on January 9, 2001. Grace Presbytery answered the overture in the negative. Attested by: /s/ Charlie H. Probst, Clerk of Session Ellisville Presbyterian Church 16. That Overture 24 from Grace Presbytery (“Set Conditions for Use of Executive Session”) be answered in the negative. Grounds: It is imprudent to restrict the use of executive session to the cases enumerated in this overture. Adopted

(to B&O) "Set Conditions for Use of Executive Session" Whereas, the Presbyterian Church in America was founded as a “grass roots” denomination; and Whereas, one of the manifestations of the “grass roots” concept is the fact that the meetings of the committees of the church were assumed to be open to all members of the church (M13GA, p. 90); and Whereas, this openness, which has been mandated by the General Assembly, is consonant with the fact that in the PCA we operate with subservient “committees” rather than semi-autonomous “boards”; and Whereas, the election of men to the various committees is an act by which the Assembly selects representatives; and Whereas, the meetings of church committees ought to be open to all the members of the denomination with the possible exception of certain highly sensitive matters, the knowledge of which being widespread might be detrimental; and Whereas, the Presbyterian Church (USA) has adopted strict guidelines for when its boards may go into executive session, so as to guarantee openness in the deliberations; and Whereas, we in the PCA should not be less open and honest than our liberal counterpart; and Whereas, this is especially the case since we self-professedly operate with committees rather than boards, as is done in the PC(USA); and Whereas, we want to preserve this openness which was set forth as the ideal in the PCA from early in its existence: Now Therefore, Be It Resolved, that Grace Presbytery hereby overtures the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America to take the following actions: 1. to reaffirm that all General Assembly committees, both permanent and ad-interim, committees of commissioners and agencies will operate in open session. 2. to require that said bodies may go into executive session only for the following reasons: property negotiations, discussion of active or pending criminal matters or civil litigation, discussion of personnel performance, personal safety, or approval of reports if required to be done in executive session. 3. to declare that whenever a committee or agency enters executive session, only the elected members and ex-officio members of that committee or agency may remain in the room, the only exception to this policy being that a person may be invited to stay if he has specific information, is otherwise involved in the matter under consideration, or not otherwise available to the committee or agency. 4. To determine that any decisions made in executive session must be reported in public and access to said decisions guaranteed to any member of the church, and that all members are guaranteed access to the minutes and official records of all committees and agencies. 5. To amend the Rules for Assembly Operation by adding a new section (4-19) to read as follows: All General Assembly committees, both permanent and ad-interim, committees of commissioners, and agencies will operate in open session. Said bodies may go into executive session only for the following reasons: property negotiations, discussion of active or pending criminal matters or civil litigation, discussion of personnel performance, personal safety, or approval of reports if required to be done in executive session. Whenever a committee or agency enters executive session, only the elected members or ex-officio members of the committee or agency may remain in the room, the only exception to this policy being that a person may be invited to stay if he has specific information, is otherwise involved in the matter under consideration, or not otherwise available to the committee or agency. Adopted by the 96th Stated Meeting of Grace Presbytery on the 11th day of January, 2001. Attested by: /s/ Eugene C. Case, Stated Clerk 17. That Overture 25 from Grace Presbytery (“Forbid Women to Preach or Teach in Corporate Worship”) be answered in the negative. Grounds: Our constitution addresses the issues sufficiently (BCO 7-2), and we do not believe our Assembly should by majority vote make a statement defining constitutional principles. Adopted

source: OVERTURE 25 From Grace Presbytery (to B&O & CCB) “Forbid Women to Preach or Teach in Corporate Worship”
body: Whereas, the Word of God and the Confessional Standards of the Presbyterian Church in America declare without ambiguity that a woman shall not teach or exercise authority over a man; and Whereas, this prohibition is proclaimed as a result of the creation ordinance and not for the reason of first century cultural expediency; and Whereas, no ecclesiastical body of the Presbyterian Church in America (be it congregation, session, presbytery, or assembly) may, under any assumed authority, set aside the clear teaching of God’s Word or the Westminster Standards; and Whereas, a contrary view to both Scripture and the Standards is being taught and adopted, specifically, that session may allow the instruction of men by women in ecclesiastical assembly under the “authority and oversight” of the elders; Therefore the Presbytery of Grace, meeting this 12th day of September, 2000, overtures the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America: 1. to affirm that a woman may not preach or teach in the corporate worship of any church or in the corporate worship conducted by any church court or by any committee, board, and/or agency of a church court; and 2. to reaffirm that the Presbyterian Church in America believes that the Scripture teaches that the offices of Elder and Deacon are open to men only. Adopted at the 98th Stated Meeting of Grace Presbytery on the 12th day of September, 2000. Attested by: /s/ Eugene C. Case, Stated Clerk 18. That Overture 27 from the Presbytery of Philadelphia (“Amend BCO 12-5e to Prohibit Women from Preaching”) be answered in the negative. Grounds: Our constitution addresses the issues sufficiently. Adopted

source: OVERTURE 27 From the Presbytery of Philadelphia (to CCB & B&O) "Amend BCO 12-5e to Prohibit Women from Preaching"
body: Whereas, there are some among us who believe that Scripture explicitly prohibits women from teaching and having authority over men in the church (1 Cor. 14:34, 35; 1 Tim. 2:11, 12); and Whereas, women may encourage each other and the children under them (Titus 2:3-5); and Whereas, our Confession explicitly and implicitly envisioned the ordinance of preaching and teaching, or "the ministry of the Word", to be limited to ordained male ministers of the Word (WCF 27.3, 4 [Scripture proofs]; LC 54 [Scripture proofs], 156, 158, 159, 169, cf. 176); and Whereas, the BCO teaches that candidates for the ministry of the Word (18-1), those licensed to the ministry of the Word (19-1), and interns who are to be ordained to the ministry of the Word (19-7) are to be males; and Whereas, BCO 19-1 teaches that "no man" can preach without licensure in the presbytery "where he will preach"; and Whereas, there are some who believe that there is considerable confusion within our church as to the proper and biblical role of women in regards to the ordinance of preaching and teaching during stated worship services; and Whereas, there are some who believe that Paul's prohibition was primarily related to the activity of teaching itself and not to the office of teaching (though it is necessarily implied, "good and necessary consequence", WCF 1:vi); and Whereas, it is impossible for women to remain silent (1 Cor. 14:34; 1 Tim. 2:12) while teaching and preaching to men during stated worship services; and Whereas, it is impossible for females to instruct men and women, to exhort from Scripture before men, or to teach or explain passages of the Bible from the pulpit during ordinary stated worship services before men and still fulfill the Biblical command of 1 Tim. 2:12 which states, "But I do not allow a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man, but to remain quiet."; and Whereas, our denomination has historically seen clearly on the issue of the role of women in the public ministry of the Word; Therefore Be It Resolved, that the General Assembly amend the BCO, par. 12-5.e d to read: To call congregational meetings when necessary; to establish and control Sunday schools and Bible classes with special reference to the children of the church; to establish and control all special groups in the church such as Men in the Church, Women in the Church and special Bible Study groups; to encourage the women of the church to hold meetings and give instruction, appropriate to their calling (e.g. Titus 2:3-5), while prohibiting women from expounding or preaching the Word of God as an ordinance of public worship (cf. BCO 4-4; 53-2), as this is clearly forbidden in Scripture (1 Tim. 2:11-12); to promote World missions; to promote obedience to the Great Commission in its totality at home and abroad; to order collections for pious uses; To exercise in accordance with the Directory for Worship, authority over the time and place of the preaching of the Word and the administration of the Sacraments, over all other religious services, over the music in the services, and over the uses to which the church building and associated properties may be put; to take the oversight of the singing in the public worship of God; to ensure that the Word of God is preached only by such as are sufficiently gifted, and also duly approved and called to that office (cf. WLC 158) and in accordance with this to prohibit women from preaching the Word of God as part of the corporate worship of the church (cf. BCO 4-4; 53-2), as this is forbidden in Scripture (1 Tim. 2:11-12); to assemble the people for worship when there is no minister; to determine the best measures for promoting the spiritual interests of the church and congregation; Adopted at the March 10, 2001, stated meeting of Philadelphia Presbytery. Attested by: /s/ Frank D. Moser, Stated Clerk 19. That Overture 28 from the Presbytery of Philadelphia (“Pray for Religious Liberty”) be answered in the affirmative, as amended. Grounds for changes: The phrase “a summary of” has been added to reduce mailing costs. The overture has been edited to make the language applicable to all members of the PCA regardless of their national origin. Adopted as amended

source: OVERTURE 28 From the Presbytery of Philadelphia
body: “Pray for Religious Liberty” (to B&O) Whereas, the PCA is a Protestant and Reformed denomination serving our God especially in the United States of America, which celebrates its 225th anniversary of Independence this July 4th, 2001, whose original states declared themselves to be committed to religious liberty and the Protestant faith as seen in the following citations from the Journal of the First Continental Congress of 1774: THAT it is an indispensable duty which we owe to God, our country, ourselves and posterity, by all lawful ways and means in our power to maintain, defend and preserve these civil and religious rights and liberties for which many of our fathers fought, bled and died, and to hand them down entire to future generations. THAT the late act of Parliament for establishing the Roman Catholic religion and the French laws in that extensive country now called Quebec, is dangerous in an extreme degree to the Protestant religion and to the civil rights and liberties of all America; and therefore as men and protestant Christians, we are indispensably obliged to take all proper measures for our security...; And in prosecution of the same system, several late, cruel and oppressive Acts have been passed respecting the town of Boston and the Massachusetts-Bay and also an Act for extending the province of Quebec, so as to border on the western frontiers of these Colonies, establishing an arbitrary government therein, and discouraging the settlement of British subjects in that wide extended country; thus by the influence of civil principles and ancient prejudices to dispose the inhabitants to act with hostility against the free Protestant Colonies, whenever a wicked Ministry shall chose so to direct them. THAT we think the Legislature of Great Britain is not authorized by the condition to establish a religion fraught with sanguinary and impious tenets, or, to erect an arbitrary form of government in any quarter of the globe. These rights we, as well as you, deem sacred. And yet sacred as they are, they have, with many others, been repeatedly and flagrantly violated... As the conclusion of the late war—a war rendered glorious by the abilities and integrity of a Minister, to whose efforts the British empire owes its safety and its fame: At the conclusion of this war, which was succeeded by an inglorious peace, formed under the auspices of a Minister of principles, and of a family unfriendly to the protestant cause, and inimical to liberty---We say at this period, and under the influence of that man, a plan for enslaving your fellow subjects in America was concerted, and has ever since been pertinaciously carrying into execution. And by another Act the dominion of Canada is to be so extended, modeled, and governed, as that by being disunited from us, detached from our interests, by civil as well as religious prejudices, that by their numbers daily swelling with Catholic emigrants from Europe, and by their devotion to Administration, so friendly to their religion, they might become formidable to us, and on occasion, to fit instruments in the hands of power, to reduce the ancient free Protestant Colonies to the same fate of slavery with themselves. The people of England will soon have an opportunity of declaring their sentiments concerning our cause. In their piety, generosity, and good sense, we repose high confidence; and cannot, upon a review of past events, be persuaded, that they, the defenders of true religion, and the assertors of the rights of mankind, will take part against their affectionate protestant brethren in the colonies, in favour of our open and their own secret enemies, whose intrigues, for several years past, have been wholly exercised in sapping the foundations of civil and religious liberty. Resolved, THAT this Congress in their own names and in behalf of all those, whom they represent, do present their most grateful acknowledgments to those truly noble, honourable and patriotic advocates of civil and religious liberty, who have so generously and powerfully, though unsuccessfully espoused and defended the cause of America, both in and out of Parliament. ...and a fourth for extending the limits of Quebec, abolishing the English and restoring the French laws, whereby great numbers of British freemen are subjected to the latter, and establishing an absolute Government and the Roman Catholic Religion throughout those vast regions, that border on the westerly and northerly boundaries of the free, protestant English settlements... And whereas, our confession, *The Westminster Confession of Faith*, declares its commitment to the idea of the liberty of the conscience, an idea developed especially by Puritans such as William Perkins and Non-conformists such as John Owen, in Chapter XX.2, “God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are, in anything, contrary to His Word; or beside it, if matters of faith, or worship. So that, to believe such doctrines, or to obey such commands, out of conscience, is to betray true liberty of conscience: and the requiring of an implicit faith, and an absolute and blind obedience, is to destroy liberty of conscience, and reason also.” And whereas, our Confession affirms the freedom of religion in XXIII. 3, Civil magistrates may not assume to themselves the administration of the Word and Sacraments; or the power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven; or, in the least, interfere in matters of faith. Yet, as nursing fathers, it is the duty of civil magistrates to protect the Church of our common Lord, without giving the preference to any denomination of Christians above the rest, in such a manner that all ecclesiastical persons whatever shall enjoy the full, free, and unquestioned liberty of discharging every part of their sacred functions, without violence or danger. And, as Jesus Christ hath appointed a regular government and discipline in his Church, no law of any commonwealth …

“Declare Denominational Employees Not Eligible For Membership On SJC” Whereas, the Presbyterian Church in America has prided itself on being a "grass roots" denomination; and Whereas, the PCA has put this principle into effect with respect to the Standing Judicial Commission (SJC) by prohibiting anyone from serving on the SJC and a Permanent Committee of the General Assembly simultaneously (BCO 15-4); and Whereas, the same principle is seen to be at work in that "Employees of the Assembly's committees or agencies are not eligible for office on an Assembly's committee or agency which administers matters directly related to their area of employment" (RAO 4-7); and Whereas, the work of the SJC covers the denomination as a whole; and Whereas, at present, four of the twenty-four members of the SJC are denominational employees; and Whereas, it seems prudent that denominational employees should not serve simultaneously on the SJC; Now Therefore, Be It Resolved, that Mid-America Presbytery hereby overtures the 29th General Assembly to declare that no denominational employee is eligible to serve on the SJC, excepting those already elected before General Assembly’s ruling on this overture; **And Be It Further Resolved** that Mid-America Presbytery hereby overtures the 29th General Assembly to amend the Rules for Assembly Operations by adding to RAO 15-1 a sentence, immediately after the first sentence, as follows: > "No one who is employed by a denominational committee or agency may serve on the Standing Judicial Commission." Adopted at the 40th Stated Meeting of Mid-America Presbytery, on April 20, 2001. Attested by: /s/ John Owen Butler, Stated Clerk 21. That **Overture 33** from TE Dan Bartel of Central Carolina Presbytery (“Call for PCA to Repent for Abandonment of Covenantal Patriarchy”) be answered in the negative. **Grounds:** 1) While affirming biblical concepts of the covenant and of the family, we do not agree with all the reasonings of and definitions in this overture. 2) No evidence is presented in the overture to support the accusation against the PCA. Adopted

But as soon as he was mighty, the large horn was broken; and in its place there came up four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven . . . And on account of transgression the host will be given over to the horn along with the regular sacrifice; and **it will fling truth to the ground and perform its will and prosper** . . . the shaggy goat represents **the kingdom of Greece**, and the large horn that is between his eyes is the first king. “And the broken horn and the four horns that arose in its place represent four kingdoms which will arise from his nation, although not with his power . . . **He will even oppose the Prince of princes** ¹¹ Plato, *The Republic*, translated by A.D. Both sexes will go to war together, and will take with them such of the children as are strong enough, that, like the children of other craftsmen, they may have a sight of what they will have to do when they are grown up.” (5:466) ¹³ Plato, *The Republic*, translated by A.D. The children of good parents, [the officers] will put into the rearing pen, handing them over to nurses who live in a particular portion of the city . . . body: "Remove Concurring Opinion in Judicial Matter 99-1" Whereas, the Western Carolina Presbytery has issued a call to the Presbyterian Church in America to bring the John Wood matter to closure and to endeavor to pursue together both the purity, peace and unity of the church; and Whereas, we question the propriety of the Standing Judicial Commission attaching concurring opinions to a report that they were not going to proceed to judicial process, since concurring opinions are provided for only in cases of judicial process and to include these concurring opinions tend to disturb the peace of the Church, after the decision has been reached; and Whereas, to allow the personal allegations against individual members of the Assembly to be placed in the Minutes of the General Assembly can only bring hurt to the individuals concerned, and cause resentments that are destructive of the purity, peace and unity of the Church; and Whereas, this is not the proper venue for such allegations, since TE's who have acted improperly should be charged in the courts of original jurisdiction, where they can have a fair trial; and Whereas, we do not believe that the provision for concurring opinions was ever intended to provide a forum for personal attack as occurs in this report; Therefore, Western Carolina Presbytery urges that all of the concurring opinions be removed from the SJC report, and that they not appear in the Minutes of the General Assembly. Adopted by Western Carolina Presbytery at a called meeting on May 8, 2001. Attested by: /s/ Skip Gillikin, Stated Clerk 23. That Personal Resolution #1 from TE H. Timothy Miessler be answered in the negative. Grounds: The phrase “under any circumstance” in lines 9 of the resolution prohibits women from teaching other women and children. (Titus 2:2-4; 2 Timothy 1:5 with 2 Timothy 3:15) Adopted Whereas, Scripture teaches that a woman is not to teach or exercise authority over a man, I Timothy 2:12 “But I do not allow a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man, but to remain quiet,”; and Whereas, Scripture states why this prohibition on women is true in 1 Timothy 2:13-15, viz., (1) Adam was created prior to Eve; (2) Adam was not deceived but Eve was; and (3) women have the management of the home and the rearing of the children as their assigned roles (Titus 2:3-5; 1 Timothy 5); and Whereas, it is an impossibility for a woman to teach “non-authoritatively” while remaining quiet; and Whereas, Scripture is authoritative in its very nature; and Whereas, a woman that expounds, exhorts, preaches, applies, lectures on, or gives an address from or based in part on Scripture, with men present, is using Scripture authoritatively over a man; and Whereas, to allow a woman to do this violates Scripture; and Whereas, the PCA is a confessional church and upholds the inerrant, infallible Word of God, the Old and New Testaments, as our “only rule of faith and obedience,” WLC Q. 3; and Whereas, we want to respect positions taken by previous General Assemblies; and Whereas, the 28th General Assembly (2000) declared that “godly men and women [may] give presentations even though they are not elders, but who in God’s providence may have insights and experience which may prove helpful and instructive to those who lead in ministry” (M28GA, pp. 101-02); and Whereas, we do not want anyone to think that the Presbyterian Church in America has taken a position that would allow women, in the presentation of their insights and experience, to expound, exhort, preach, apply, lecture on, or give an address from or based in part on Scripture, particularly to a mixed audience; and Whereas, recent events may have given that impression; and Whereas, it is important that we be as clear as possible in our positions; and Whereas, in the past, General Assemblies have clarified positions taken by previous Assemblies (cf. M8GA, p. 97); Therefore Be It Resolved, that the 29th General Assembly clarify the position taken by the 28th General Assembly by declaring that Scripture prohibits a woman, under any circumstance, from publicly expounding, exhorting, applying, or preaching the Word of God. 24. “Ask AC to Provide Options for Lower Costs and Greater RE Participation at General Assembly” Whereas, the PCA has from its inception subscribed to the parity of Elders, and, Whereas, since the first GA in 1973 when the enrollment was 208 Ruling Elders and 179 Teaching Elders, the disparity, between Ruling Elders and Teaching Elders has grown to as many as 2 ½ Teaching Elders to 1 Ruling Elder (2.5 to 1) at some Assemblies; and, Whereas, the rising costs associated with attending GA has become a burden for many churches; therefore they send only one Commissioner and he is the pastor; and, Whereas, the perception of congregations is that General Assembly is a time for Teaching Elders to renew friendships rather than being on the floor and participating in the business of the Church; and, Whereas, Ruling Elders do not have the advantage of knowing others attending; in comparison to Teaching Elders who have developed friendships in seminary and other ministry opportunities; and, Whereas, many of the Ruling Elders are frustrated by parliamentary, maneuvering and/or debate over semantics and technical points; and, Whereas, many Ruling Elders subsequently become discouraged and choose not to return; and, Whereas, the expenses for Ruling Elders are greater than the Teaching Elders (i.e. the RE often must use vacation and/or personal time; some self-employed are required to hire a substitute for them [increasing their personal cost]; and others often pay all the expenses related to GA from their personal account); and, Whereas, previous assemblies (M16GA, p. 211) instructed the Administrative Committee (Stated Clerk's Office) to contract with motels, and/or convention centers in locations where pornographic and other questionable programming are not available: and. Whereas, it is becoming more difficult to find such locations; and, Whereas, previous Assemblies indicated their desire for facilities with Air Conditioning and other amenities; and. Whereas, the opportunity for the Administrative Committee to negotiate contracts with motels etc. to host GA is limited; therefore adding to the rising costs; THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Administrative Committee report to the 30th General Assembly in 2002 with recommendations and possible options how the General Assembly can have greater parity. between elders while keeping the costs of GA as low as possible for final approval by the Assembly understanding that options before us may require the Assembly to approve significant changes so that costs may be reduced and greater involvement of Ruling Elders achieved. Steven Meyerhoff Stated Clerk Dear Dr. Meyerhoff: I am in receipt of your letter of April 15 stating Westminster Presbytery’s request that that Overture #7 from Westminster Presbytery be assigned by me to the Committee of Commissioners on Bills and Overtures. It would be contrary to the “Rules of Assembly Operations” for me to accede to your request. 10-5. Upon receipt the Stated Clerk shall refer to the Committee on Constitutional Business all overtures requesting amendment of the Book of Church Order. Upon receipt the Stated Clerk shall forward all overtures concerning presbytery boundaries or a new presbytery to the Subcommittee on Boundaries appointed by and under the jurisdiction of the Assembly’s permanent Committee on Mission to North America which shall report to the Permanent Committee and shall report to the Assembly through the Committee of Commissioners on Mission to North America. All other overtures shall be referred by the Clerk to the appropriate Committee of Commissioners. All overtures shall be printed in the Handbook with reference for consideration indicated. 13-1. All business shall ordinarily come to the floor of the Assembly for final action through Committees of Commissioners, except reports of the Standing Judicial Commission, the Committee on Constitutional Business, the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records, the Nominating Committee, and Ad Interim Committees, which shall report directly to the Assembly. The following Committees of Commissioners shall handle the matters indicated: Reports of Overtures, Committees, Resolutions or Communications 1. Administration Permanent Comm. Touching Administrative matters 2. Bills and Overtures of general nature 3. Christian Education Permanent Comm. Touching Christian and Publications Education Publications 4. Covenant College Trustees Touching Covenant College 5. Covenant Seminary Trustees Touching Covenant Seminary 6. Insurance & Annuities Trustees Touching insurance & annuities 7. Interchurch Permanent Comm. Touching comity, Relations cooperation relations to other churches 8. Mission to North America Permanent Comm. Touching home missions 9. Mission to the World Permanent Comm. Touching world missions 10. PC A Foundation Trustees Touching PC A Foundation 11. Ridge Haven Directors Touching Ridge Haven You may recall that a similar request was made in 2000 that the Westminster Overture #20 “Reject Covenant College’s Response to Protest” be considered by the Committee of Commissioners on Bills and Overtures rather than the Committee of Commissioners on Covenant College. The Stated Clerk did not accede to that request on the same basis as cited above, namely “RAO” 10-5 and 13-1. The General Assembly sustained the Clerk’s referral. I do not have the authority to contravene or ignore the “RAO.” Insofar as I know, the only way to refer Overture #7 to the Committee of Commissioners on Bills and Overtures would be to suspend the “RAO.” ARTICLE XVIII. AMENDMENT OR SUSPENSION OF RULES The Rules of Assembly Operations may be amended or suspended only by a two-thirds vote of those voting which must also be a majority of the total enrollment of commissioners. A motion to amend is debatable. A motion to suspend is not debatable. In short, it would be contrary to the “Rules of Assembly Operations” for me to accede to your request. Sincerely, /s/ L. Roy Taylor Stated Clerk, PCA COMMUNICATION 4 from Westminster Presbytery “Westminster Rescinds Withdrawal, Will Remain in PCA” Dear Fathers and Brethren, Greetings in the matchless name of our Savior, Jesus Christ! We want to thank you for all the time, effort, and energy that you have spent on our Presbytery over the past couple of years. As you know, we have had a difficult time wrestling with how to deal with theological and ideological differences among us. Although there are numerous issues about which not all of us agree, nevertheless, we are happy to report that there has been a sweeter spirit in our meetings over the past year or so. We believe that this is due to the prayers of God’s people, and we thank you for all the prayers which you have offered up on our behalf. In January of this year, our Presbytery voted to rescind its determination to withdraw from the Presbyterian Church in America. The motion carried overwhelmingly, with less than a handful of votes against it. This is a truly remarkable occurrence. We appreciate the pleading of the 29th General Assembly, as expressed in its pastoral letter to us, that we reconsider our intention to break the ties of fellowship, and we are happy to report that we have indeed determined to continue to walk together with our denomination. Our determination to remain in the Presbyterian Church in America is reflective of our desire that the PCA become a leader church for our culture in the twenty-first century. We believe that there are tremendous challenges for the Body of Christ in this new millennium, from ethical issues (cloning, for example), to persecution of God’s people, to the threat of false religious systems (including Islam and Roman Catholicism). body: action: 1) “To instruct the PCAF that it must allow members of the General Assembly to inspect the records in accord with the denominational corporation charter and Delaware state law;” 2) “To instruct all of the committees and agencies, including those that may be separately incorporated, of the rights of the members of the General Assembly in this regard;” 3) “That if (the General Assembly) is unable to assert its rightful ownership of and oversight over these agencies, the Assembly begin the process of divesting itself of these agencies.” Grounds: Request 1 [see text below]: 1. The PCAF is fully under and submissive to the General Assembly in all the provisions of the BCO, RAO and its own by-laws and articles of incorporation. 2. This authority and submission is implemented by the Board of Trustees elected at-large by the General Assembly and the work of the Committee of Commissioners and their report to the General Assembly and the subsequent actions of the GA. 3. The Overture originates from a request for information that was denied by the PCAF Board of Trustees in accordance with the General Assembly approved “Confidentiality Policy.” 4. The Overture cites Delaware Civil law; however, the PCAF is incorporated under Georgia law. 5. The Overture appears to use civil law to circumvent the ecclesiastical government of the General Assembly over the PCAF and other Committees and Agencies. Request 2 [see text below]: we deem it as unnecessary because the General Assembly already has a system of oversight. The committees and agencies of the PCA are already submissive to the General Assembly in all the provisions of the BCO and RAO and their own respective bylaws, articles of incorporation or manuals of operations. Request 3 [see text below]: The General Assembly has and does continue to maintain proper oversight over its committees and agencies.

source: OVERTURE 7 from Westminster Presbytery (to PCAF & AC)
body: “Allow Inspection of PCAF and All Other Committee and Agency Records by Individuals or General Assembly Divest Itself of Committees and Agencies” Whereas, the PCA Foundation was formed by the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America; and Whereas, the PCA Foundation is a constituent part of the Presbyterian Church in America, and all of the members of the PCA Foundation Board are elected by the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America (Corporate Bylaws of Presbyterian Church in America (A Corporation), Article VI.5); Whereas, the intimate connection between the Foundation and the denomination is seen even in the ability of the Board of the Foundation to designate a member of the Administrative Committee of the General Assembly (,BCO 14-1-12); and Whereas, the PCA Foundation, which was originally a subcommittee, gained separate agency status in 1983, similar to other agencies, such as Covenant College, Covenant Theological Seminary, Ridge Haven, and Insurance, Annuities, and Relief (M9GA, p. 116, 8.e; Ml 1GA, p. 113, 1.); and Whereas, the provisions regarding Covenant College and Covenant Theological Seminary in 1983 included the following: “Since the General Assembly is responsible for the conduct of the work which the whole church does unitedly, the powers and activities that it has delegated to institutions under its jurisdiction shall always be subject to review. It shall not delegate any of its general powers beyond its own recall so as to cease to be fully responsible for the spiritual oversight of the entire denomination” (M9GA, p, 100, 5.i); and Whereas, recent correspondence from the PCA Foundation, indicates that the PCA Foundation is maintaining that the right of a member of the denominational corporation to inspect the records does not include the right to inspect the records of the PCA Foundation; and Whereas, the position taken by the PCA Foundation would mean that it is no longer under the effective control of the General Assembly; and Whereas, while we have no grounds to believe that there is presently any malfeasance being practiced by the PCA Foundation, nevertheless, in order to maintain proper checks and balances, the General Assembly itself, and by extension the members thereof, must have the ability to inspect the records of the PCA Foundation; and Whereas, the position taken by the PCA Foundation, if not corrected by the General Assembly, will imply that any and all denominational corporations will no longer be subject to General Assembly control, but will essentially be autonomous agencies; and Whereas, we have an obligation, corporately and individually, to exercise oversight of the denominational agencies, and it would be malfeasance on our part to refuse to assert our oversight responsibility; Now therefore be it resolved, that Westminster Presbytery hereby overtures the 30th General Assembly, meeting in Birmingham, Alabama, in June, 2002, to instruct the PCA Foundation that it must allow members of the General Assembly to inspect the records in accord with the denominational corporation charter and Delaware state law; And be it further resolved, that Westminster Presbytery hereby overtures the 30lh General Assembly to instruct all of the committees and agencies, including those that may be separately incorporated, of the rights of the members of the General Assembly in this regard; And be it further resolved, that Westminster Presbytery hereby overtures the 30th General Assembly that if it is unable to assert its rightful ownership of and oversight over these agencies, the Assembly begin the process of divesting itself of these agencies.

body: Westminster Standards ” It is the opinion of the CCB that the proposed constitutional language creates constitutional conflicts with the BCO Preliminary Principles. Furthermore, the proposed language creates constitutional ambiguity. 1. The proposed overture language “either in his private life” is in conflict with BCO Preliminary Principle II. 1 and II.7. 2. The proposed overture language requiring Presbyteries to record every man’s views disagreeing with the Constitution will erode the Presbyteries’ exclusive authority to determine if a candidate receives and adopts the Confession of Faith and the Catechism of the PCA as containing the system of doctrine taught in the Holy Scriptures. See BCO 21-5. This is in conflict with BCO Preliminary Principle II.2 that recognizes the right of each court to determine its membership. (BCO Preface II.2, BCO 21-1 through 7; BCO 13-1; BCO 13-9 a,c,d; BCO 11-3 & 4). 3. An ambiguity created by the proposed language is the introduction of the phrase: “exception to the standards.” This phrase is nowhere else found in our constitution. The phrase elicits a plethora of interpretations, many of which go beyond our present Constitutional parameters. 4. It has not normally been the mission of the CCB to decide on the placement of Constitutional language. [For text and action, see 30-50, III, 3, p. 238.] Adopted by CCB

Specific areas of conflict include, but are not limited to: 1. The Overture would allow a General Assembly to avoid the provisions of the BCO without appropriate constitutional process and would result in serious constitutional uncertainty. (BCO 26-2). 2. The Overture allows modification of virtually any action of the General Assembly or commission thereof, with the sole limitation that an actual judgment of a judicial commission may not be changed or deleted, thereby undermining the very principle of orderly Church Government which the BCO is designed to protect. [See Appendix A, p. 346.] V. Review of Minutes of the Standing Judicial Commission 1. SJC Minutes Nov. 29, 2001, p. 21 ff. Response: In accordance with SJC Manual 20.5, the CCB approves the minutes of the Nov. 29, 2001 meeting of the Standing Judicial Commission (SJC) as being in conformity to the Manual of the SJC and mo 15. Editorial notations regarding form (e.g., punctuation and format) were passed to the Stated Clerk. 2. SJC Minutes March 7, 2002, p. 31 ff. Response: We postpone action on the March 7, 2002 minutes of the SJC and respectfully request the SJC to request more time of the General Assembly and/or reconsider its action “to draft and present to the 30th General Assembly procedures to be placed in the SJC Manual for examining concurring and dissenting opinions to be sure that such opinions are in temperate language ...“ prior to the final report that the CCB makes to the GA. 3. Procedure for Hearing a Memorial Response: It is the advice of CCB that the “Procedure for Hearing a Memorial'’ raises significant constitutional issues. These issues include: 1) our concern that the procedures may reflect a definition of a memorial inconsistent with our historical Presbyterian usage since no clear definition is offered and the term has been variously used in other/former denominations ina manner that allows a higher court to act for a lower court. 2) The lack of clear BCO or SJC Manual definition of what constitutes a “memorial” being “administratively in order.” 3) Significant questions of due process such as the preclusion of appropriate briefing and argument. As an editorial note, we also remind the Stated Clerk that if the changes proposed by the SJC relating to new SJC Manual section 18 are approved, then the present references to SJC Manual 18 in SJC Manual 13-9 (and potentially other places) will need to be RE numbered. Other conforming changes may also be needed. Respectfully Submitted; Respectfully Submitted; /s/ TE Craig Childs, Chairman /s/ RE Richard Springer, Secretary SUPPLEMENTAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTIONAL BUSINESS A. It was MSP to amend the CCB’s report concerning its response to the SJC’s proposed manual amendment entitled, “Procedure for Hearing a Memorial,’ such that the CCB response in Paragraph 3 of section v of its report was beyond the scope of RAO 15.1 and therefore, the report of the CCB is hereby amended by striking therefrom Paragraph 3 of Section V in its entirety. B. Considered a constitutional inquiry from Philadelphia Presbytery: “At its May 11, 2002, stated meeting, Philadelphia Presbytery voted to make a constitutional inquiry to the Constitutional Business Committee of the General Assembly, to wit: having accepted an appeal from a church member against a judgment rendered against him by the session of his church, and having referred that appeal to a duly appointed commission properly erected by Presbytery, does the Presbytery have the right: 1. to take back from said commission the matter committed to it before the commission can complete its task and render a judgment; and 2. to reverse, without hearing the appeal, the decision of the Session, which found the appellant guilty and suspended him from the office of ruling elder? The actual case in dispute has been in the commission's hands for sixteen months and the record of the case has still not be enable to be finalized to the satisfaction of the appellant, the session, and the commission. Philadelphia Presbytery’ needs and requests the advice of our fathers and brothers. ” It is the opinion of the CCB that in reference to question #1 of the inquiry, our answer is yes, the Presbytery may take back from said commission the matter committed to it before the commission has completed its task and rendered a judgment. In reference to question #2, our answer is no, the Presbytery may not reverse, without hearing the appeal, the decision of the Session. The Presbytery must follow the procedures detailed in BCO 42. Respectfully Submitted, /s/ TE Craig D. Childs, Sr., Chairman /si TE Mark A. Rowden, Acting Secretary SECOND SUPPLEMENTAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTIONAL BUSINESS 1. Received a constitutional inquiry asking CCB to give advice on the constitutionality of the Committee of Commissioners recommendation #15. The question posed for CCB was as follows, Is it constitutional for the General Assembly to adopt the following recommendation: That the General Assembly mandate coverage in the PCA health plans for all active ministers and church lay employees who are current residents of the United States and who are not covered under a spouse’s group health plan, and that the Presbyteries be responsible for implementing this mandate. The CCB answered: No. It is the opinion of the CCB that in the absence of any evidence from BCO 14, the Westminster Confession of Faith and Catechisms, or Scripture as to the right of the General Assembly to make such a requirement; the General Assembly may not mandate coverage in the PCA health plan. body: “Form Blue Ridge Presbytery” Whereas the churches of New River Presbytery located within the Commonwealth of Virginia have for some time prayed about, considered, and most recently held planning meetings (including several churches in James River and Potomac Presbyteries) concerning the establishment of a new Presbytery in western Virginia, and Whereas the demographic, sociological and economic connections of churches throughout western Virginia - principally along and to the west of the Blue Ridge Mountains - make working together as a Presbytery highly desirable, and Whereas the churches currently located in western Virginia have discovered that they are of one mind in their desire to do church planting in this region, as well as develop an enlarged work of Reformed University Ministries among the many colleges and universities in this region (in addition to the other normal functions of a Presbytery), and, Whereas, while the remaining churches located in West Virginia fall just short of the minimum membership and attendance goals, they have a special cohesiveness that their leadership believes will enable them to overcome their somewhat small size, Therefore, New River Presbytery, meeting at Nitro, West Virginia in its stated meeting of March 9th, 2002, hereby overtures the 30th General Assembly that, effective September 1, 2002 a new Presbytery of the Blue Ridge be formed by the division of New River Presbytery (along with churches from James River Presbytery and Potomac Presbytery - see separate overtures) as follows: a. New Boundaries of New River Presbytery: “All of West Virginia except for the counties of Morgan, Berkeley and Jefferson.” b. Boundaries of the newly formed Blue Ridge Presbytery: “All churches and missions in Virginia, bounded on the north and east and including the counties (and contained independent cities) of Frederick, Clarke, Fauquier, Culpeper, Orange, Louisa, Fluvanna, Albemarle, Nelson, Appomattox, Campbell, and Pittsylvania and bounded on the west and including the counties of Giles, Pulaski, and Carroll (east of 1-77). c. Revised boundaries of James River Presbytery will be as follows: “All of Virginia south and east of and including the following counties, except for the counties of Accomac and Northampton on the Eastern Shore: Northumberland, Westmoreland, King George, Stafford, Spotsylvania, Hanover, Goochland, Cumberland, Buckingham, Prince Edward, Charlotte, and Halifax.” d. Revised Virginia boundaries of Potomac Presbytery will be as follows: “The Virginia counties of Arlington, Fairfax, Prince William, and Loudoun, including the cities within their borders.” 9. That Overture 8 from James River Presbytery be answered by referring to Recommendation 8. Adopted

body: “Revise Boundaries of James River Presbytery” Whereas, having been appraised by formal overture of the desire of several of the churches in our Presbytery located in the western area of Virginia desiring to unite with the newly forming Presbytery of the Blue Ridge, and Whereas, having reviewed the proposed overture from New River Presbytery asking the General Assembly to establish this new Presbytery, and Whereas, having reviewed the proposed new boundaries of James River Presbytery contained in this proposed overture from New River Presbytery, Therefore be it resolved that James River Presbytery, voting at Hopewell, Virginia in the One Hundred and Fifth Stated Meeting of January 19, 2002 does hereby approve of the following change to our boundaries effective September 1, 2002: Revised boundaries of James River Presbytery will be as follows: “All of Virginia south and east of and including the following counties, except for the counties of Accomac and Northampton on the Eastern Shore: Northumberland, Westmoreland, King George, Stafford, Spotsylvania, Hanover, Goochland, Cumberland, Buckingham, Prince Edward, Charlotte, and Halifax.” 10. That the General Assembly give thanks to the Lord for the generous response of the churches and members of the PCA to the special needs resulting from the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in New York City and Washington, D.C. And that the General Assembly give thanks for God’s grace through the network of PCA churches in the metropolitan cities who were able and willing to minister to their communities in significant ways. Further, that churches be encouraged: • To develop plans for ministry in case disasters should occur in their communities, including ministry not only to PCA families, but to other members of the Body of Christ, as well as ministries proclaiming Christ’s mercy in Word and deed to those outside the Body of Christ. • To respond with generous giving when appeals for disaster response are issued through MNA for disasters occurring in the United States and Canada. Churches and individuals are encouraged to give through MNA, in order to reduce accounting and recipient costs for recipient churches and presbyteries, noting that MNA charges no administrative fees for the channeling of these gifts .Adopted 14. That Overture 13 from Session of Faith Reformed Presbyterian Church be answered in the negative. Adopted Rationale: • This overture originated from the Session of Faith Reformed Church in Fairmont, W. Virginia. It was rejected by New River Presbytery. Per RAO 10-10, the Session forwarded the overture to General Assembly. • Two other PCA churches are located in the counties which this Session asks to have moved to Pittsburgh Presbytery. These two churches are opposed to the change. Thus, of the three churches directly affected by the change, two are opposed. • Pittsburgh Presbytery has not taken any action on this change.

body: “Redraw New York State Presbytery Boundary” Whereas, the current western boundary of the New York State Presbytery includes central New York east and including Monroe, Ontario, Livingston and Steuben counties; and, Whereas, the current eastern boundary of the Ascension Presbytery includes western New York west and including Orleans, Genesee, Wyoming, and Allegany counties; and, Whereas, the Presbyterian Church of Wellsville and its teaching elder desires to leave the Ascension Presbytery and affiliate with New York State Presbytery; and Whereas, the Presbyterian Church of Wellsville is located in Allegany county which is currently within the boundary of the Ascension Presbytery; and, Whereas, the New York State Presbytery desires to receive the Presbyterian Church of Wellsville and its teaching elder; and Whereas, the New York State Presbytery desires to initiate and oversee the planting of healthy and reproducing PCA churches in every major city in upstate New York including Buffalo; and Therefore, Be It Resolved that the New York State Presbytery hereby overtures the 30th General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America to redraw the western boundary of New York State Presbytery and the northeastern New York boundary of Ascension Presbytery, to wit, that the counties currently belonging to the Ascension Presbytery which are in New York State be transferred to New York State Presbytery, thus having all the churches and counties within the geographical bounds of New York State, excepting those churches and counties belonging to Metropolitan New York Presbytery, within New York State Presbytery to be effective July 1, 2002 .

source: OVERTURE 19 from Chesapeake Presbytery (to B&O & AC)
body: “Erect a Study Committee on Ministry Amidst Ethnic Diversity” Whereas Christ calls us to penetrate cultural boundaries with the gospel, and consequently embrace the multi cultural fellowship our Lord creates, and Whereas our own nation has not escaped the ravages of racism and ethnic oppression that typically afflict our fallen world, and Whereas Chesapeake Presbytery adopted the following affirmations at its stated meeting on 16 February 2002 : Affirmations of Ethnic Diversity. 1. Evangelism of people from various racial backgrounds and social classes, with the accompanying reconciliation of such believers in the Body, is an essential element of the Church’s calling to preach the Gospel (Acts 15). 2. A faithful presentation of the gospel to the particular people groups in our region demands cultural sensitivity (1 Cor 9:19-23). 3. The gospel that reconciles Jews and Gentiles in the New Testament is the same gospel that reconciles all believers regardless of race and class. This work of reconciliation is not optional (Gal. 3:26-29; Eph. 2:14-18; Col. 3:11). 4. We must guard against superficial unity that is an affront to the dignity of God’s image bearers and damages an authentic presentation of the gospel (Acts 6:1-7). 5. Our leaders and church members need to be equipped in order to reach the diverse people of their changing cultural environment (Eph. 4:1-13). 6. We confess and repent of sins of disunity (racism, prejudice, injustice, ethnic superiority, bitterness, lack of forgiveness, cultural idolatries, etc.,) (Gal. 2:11; 1 Cor 11:17-22; James 2:1-7). 7. The church must have a continued infusion of the grace of the gospel, through prayer, the preaching of the Word and the celebration of the sacraments in the power of the Spirit, in order effectively implement the biblical principles of unity (Eph 3:14-19; Acts 20:32). 8. The power of the Spirit through the ministry of the Word equips God’s people to become a transforming community characterized by love for Christ and one another. 9. We celebrate our unity in Christ with all those who embrace the gospel. Whereas Chesapeake Presbytery also adopted the following applications at its stated meeting on 16 February 2002: Applications of Ethnic Diversity. 1. Communicate to all approved seminaries Presbytery’s recommendation that if urban, cross-cultural ministry and ethnic church history do not find a place in the core curriculum for M.Div. students, that the Seminary consider adding such subjects. 2. Direct the Committee on Christian Education to make urban and cross-cultural ministry training a part of the internship curriculum. 3. Direct the Committee on Christian Education, in partnership with the Committee on Mission to North America, to prepare a guide to readings and other resources in urban and cross-cultural ministry to assist in equipping local churches and lay leadership to reach the people groups in their target regions. 4. Direct the Committee on Mission to North America to pursue church planting strategies that are sensitive to the ethnic and cultural diversity of the region. 5. Direct the Committee on Reformed University Ministries to encourage present works and develop new works that are sensitive to the ethnic and cultural diversity of the region. 6. Encourage all elders of the Presbytery to renewed diligence in setting before the people of our churches the Scriptural calling to pursue mercy and justice. And Whereas Potomac Presbytery has adopted similar affirmations and applications, and Whereas the challenges of ministry amidst increasing ethnic diversity has been much on the mind of one or more other Presbyteries in the PCA, Therefore, Chesapeake Presbytery overtures the 30th General Assembly of the PCA to erect a special study committee to: 1) Explore the challenges presented to our ministry by the increasing ethnic diversity of our nation, 2) Suggest ways our General Assembly Committees, Presbyteries, and churches might meet these challenges, 3) Offer a statement of biblical values and commitments declaring to God, to the world, and to ourselves our convictions in these matters.

source: OVERTURE 5 from Ohio Valley Presbytery (to CCB & B&O)
body: and Metropolitan New York Presbytery, Uliana Presbytery, Missouri Presbytery, Piedmont Triad Presbytery, North Georgia Presbytery, Evangel Presbytery, Fellowship Presbytery, Tennessee Valley Presbytery, Rocky Mountain Presbytery, North Texas Presbytery, Nashville Presbytery, Susquehanna Valley Presbytery, Northern California Presbytery, North Florida Presbytery, Heartland Presbytery, Central Florida Presbytery, Northern Illinois Presbytery, South Texas Presbytery and Southeast Alabama Presbytery “Require Ten Percent of Presbyteries to Assume Original Jurisdiction Over a Minister in BCO 34-1 - Version 1” Whereas, the grassroots history of the Presbyterian Church in America indicates her desire to act in unity with the consensus of her churches; and Whereas, the present wording of Book of Church Order 34-1 allows only two presbyteries to require the General Assembly to decide whether to assume original jurisdiction in judicial process against a minister in another Presbytery; and Whereas, this standard can allow presbyteries of a particular perspective, and potentially quite few churches, to challenge the ordinary rights of a Presbytery to determine its own membership according to the men and circumstances best known by the local Presbytery; and Whereas, this standard, in effect, can allow two presbyteries and a few churches, to bring charges against one or many presbyters across Presbytery boundaries and potentially to flood the General Assembly with charges that express the concerns of very few; and Whereas, such narrow concerns should not be allowed to challenge the ordinary rights of any Presbytery to determine its own membership unless there is a wide consensus in the church that a Presbytery has failed to act properly; Therefore, to ensure that a small minority of presbyteries or churches does not exercise inordinate influence over other churches, presbyteries and the General Assembly in pursuing the discipline of ministers; and to ensure that there is a significant indication of a likely consensus in the denomination that the GA must assume original jurisdiction in such a case for the sake of the purity and testimony of the church, Ohio Valley Presbytery / Metropolitan New York Presbytery / Illiana Presbytery / Missouri Presbytery / Piedmont Triad Presbytery / North Georgia Presbytery / Evangel Presbytery / Fellowship Presbytery / Tennessee Valley Presbytery / Rocky Mountain Presbytery / North Texas Presbytery / Nashville Presbytery / Susquehanna Valley Presbytery / Northern California Presbytery / North Florida Presbytery / Heartland Presbytery / Central Florida Presbytery / Northern Illinois Presbytery / South Texas Presbytery / Southeast Alabama Presbytery overtures the General Assembly to amend the Book of Church Order by changing the words “two other” in BCO 34-1 to “at least ten percent of all the Presbyteries.”

source: OVERTURE 18 from Potomac Presbytery (to CCB & B&O)
body: “Amend Both BCO 33-1 and 34-1 to Require Greater Consensus to Assume Original Jurisdiction Over Members and Ministers” Whereas the history of the Presbyterian Church in America, with respect to the former denominational connection of many of its officers and congregations, indicates the great importance of the voice of a minority in attempts to preserve the faithfulness of a denomination; whereas the present wording of the Book of Church Order wisely makes provision for the correction of one court through the efforts of others of like grade, through an appeal to a more inclusive court; Whereas the grassroots history of the Presbyterian Church in America indicates her desire to act in unity with the consensus of her churches; whereas the present wording of Book of Church Order of 33- 1 allows two Sessions to require a Presbytery to assume original jurisdiction injudicial process against a member in another congregation, and BCO 34-1 allows two presbyteries to require the General Assembly to assume original jurisdiction in judicial process against a minister in another Presbytery; Whereas, as the Presbyterian Church in America grows, this standard, expressed in a fixed number, will allow an increasingly smaller representation of the denomination to challenge the ordinary rights of a Session or Presbytery to fulfill its Constitutional duties; Whereas the ordinary rights of a court to fulfill its constitutional responsibilities should not be liable to challenge unless there is a significant proportion in the church that is persuaded that a court has failed to act properly; and Whereas the parallel provisions (BCO 33-1 and BCO 34-1) have slightly different language, which may lead to confusion, and any change introduced in the standard of one section should reasonably be introduced in the other on similar grounds; Therefore, to ensure that a disproportionate representation of churches or presbyteries does not exercise undue influence over other churches, presbyteries and the General Assembly in pursuing discipline; and, to ensure that there is a significant indication of the need for a higher court to assume original jurisdiction in such a case for the sake of the purity and testimony of the church, Potomac Presbytery overtures the 30th General Assembly to amend The Book of Church Order as follows: 1. In BCO 33-1, strike the words “two other” and add in that place “at least five percent, but not less than two, of all of the” so that the section reads: and at least five percent, but not less than two, of all of the Sessions of churches in the same Presbytery request the Presbytery of which the church is a member to initiate proper or appropriate action in a case of process and thus assume jurisdiction and authority, the Presbytery shall do so. and 2. In BCO 34-1, strike the words, “and two other Presbyteries request the General Assembly to assume original jurisdiction (to first receive and initially hear and determine), the General Assembly shall do so.” and add in that place: and at least five percent of all of the Presbyteries request the General Assembly to initiate proper or appropriate action in a case of process and thus assume jurisdiction and authority, the General Assembly shall do so.
