and Gwinnett county south of the defined boundaries, from east to west, of Highway 316, then Sugarloaf Parkway to Peachtree Industrial Boulevard, then an imaginary line westward from the intersection of Peachtree Industrial Boulevard and Sugarloaf Parkway to the Chattahoochee River; **Therefore, be it resolved** that Georgia Foothills Presbytery overtures the 52 [nd] General Assembly as follows: - That Lumpkin County be transferred from Metro Atlanta Presbytery to Georgia Foothills Presbytery; - By adding Lumpkin County to the list of Georgia counties included within the boundary of Georgia Foothills Presbytery; and - By removing Lumpkin County from the list of Georgia counties included within the boundary of Metro Atlanta Presbytery. _Adopted by Georgia Foothills Presbytery at its stated meeting, April 15,_ _2025_ _Attested by TE Don Aldin, stated clerk_

source: OVERTURE 37 from the Southeast Alabama Presbytery (to CCB, OC)
body: “Amend _BCO_ 12-3 so that a Session May Elect One of Its Members as Moderator in Judicial Cases” **Be it resolved** that _BCO_ 12-3 is amended as follows (underlining for additions; strikethrough for deletions): **12-3.** when a church is without a pastor, the moderator of the Session may be either a minister appointed for that purpose by the Presbytery, with consent of the Session, or one invited by the Session to preside on a particular occasion, or one of its own members elected to preside. In judicial cases, the Session may elect one of its members to preside as moderator shall be a or invite a minister of the presbytery to which the church belongs to preside as moderator. So that _BCO_ 12-3 as amended would read: **12-3.** when a church is without a pastor, the moderator of the Session may be either a minister appointed for that purpose by the Presbytery, with consent of the Session, or one invited by the Session to preside on a particular occasion, or one of its own members elected to preside. In judicial cases, the Session may elect one of its members to preside as moderator or invite a minister of the Presbytery to which the church belongs to preside as moderator. **RATIONALE:** Sessions should have discretion to elect a moderator in judicial cases. Some Sessions may have ruling elders who are highly experienced in church discipline and cases of process, and they should have the liberty to elect such a ruling elder to preside. In instances where this is not the case, the revised provision retains the right of the Session to invite a minister of the Presbytery to preside. _Adopted by the Southeast Alabama Presbytery at its stated meeting, April 22,_ _2025_ _Attested by TE Kevin Corley, stated clerk_

source: OVERTURE 38 from the Southeast Alabama Presbytery (to CCB, OC)
body: “Amend _BCO_ 30-4 to Require a New Case with Process for Elevation of Indefinite Suspension to Excommunication” **Be it resolved** that _BCO_ 30-4 be amended as follows (underlining for additions): **30-4.** Excommunication is the excision of an offender from the communion of the Church. This censure is to be inflicted only on account of gross crime or heresy and when the offender shows himself incorrigible and contumacious. Elevating indefinite suspension from the Sacraments to excommunication shall require a new case of process establishing that the matter is a gross crime or heresy and that the offender has shown himself incorrigible and contumacious. The design of this censure is to operate on the offender as a means of reclaiming him, to deliver the church from the scandal of his offense, and to inspire all with fear by the example of his discipline. So that _BCO_ 30-4 as amended would read: **30-4.** Excommunication is the excision of an offender from the communion of the Church. This censure is to be inflicted only on account of gross crime or heresy and when the offender shows himself incorrigible and contumacious. Elevating indefinite suspension from the Sacraments to excommunication shall require a new case of process establishing that the matter is a gross crime or heresy and that the offender has shown himself incorrigible and contumacious. The design of this censure is to operate on the offender as a means of reclaiming him, to deliver the church from the scandal of his offense, and to inspire all with fear by the example of his discipline. **RATIONALE:** The SJC recently decided _TE Aaron Myers v. Iliana Presbytery_ ( _M51GA_, 2024, pages 824-834) in which it concluded that where there is a previous finding of guilt and imposition of censure, a censured person is not entitled to full process _de novo_ for the court to find him “incorrigible and contumacious” ( _BCO_ 30-4). The SJC, invoking the “intrinsic powers” of our courts and “parliamentary law,” prescribed the following procedure: the indefinitely suspended person has aright to a hearing in the matter: he must be charged by the court supervising the indefinite suspension with being “incorrigible and contumacious,” he must be presented with the evidence to that effect, he must be called upon to plead before the court, and he would have aright to a defense before the original trial court. The court, upon completing its hearing, would be called upon to consider a motion to amend a matter previously adopted, to elevate the indefinite suspension to excommunication. Passage would require a two thirds majority (2/3), unless previous notice were given of an intent to offer a motion to amend a matter previously adopted, the notice framed in such a way as to avoid undermining the impartiality of the maker and thereby disqualifying him from participation in the hearing. This procedure is not expressly prescribed anywhere in our Rules of Discipline. the SJC previously treated a decision to elevate censure as a matter of its discretion without the necessity of further process in _Dallison v. North Florida_ _Presbytery_, ( _M30GA_ 2002, page 156, 160-161). As in _Myers_, _Dallison_ denied that the Constitution requires a “new trial for new charges” for elevating censure but afforded the court “discretion” in such elevations of censure (subject to the “clear error” standard). But _Dallison_ never mentioned limiting that discretion by a parliamentary procedure as the SJC only recently held in _Myers_, evidencing an ongoing lack of certainty and uniformity in the standards our courts should apply when imposing the Church’s highest censure in elevation cases. Contrary to the variable holdings on display in _Myers_ and _Dallison_, before a member of the Church is excommunicated, he should be afforded a regular case of process per our Rules of Discipline to guarantee that those conditions peculiarly pertinent to excommunication have been established in accordance with the time-tested procedures that Presbyterianism has long recognized as decent and fair. Such procedures ensure a meaningful record is made detailing the ground for the court’s decision and affording an excommunicated person a meaningful final review of his excommunication. Since the accused’s restoration to the Sacraments is the intended result of indefinite suspension and excommunication alike, the real difference between the two censures is whether the accused has any right of review, a hollow right indeed in the absence of the protections afforded by a case of process. Importantly, a person under indefinite suspension from the Sacraments has no right to complain against a court’s refusal to restore him, however meritorious his case may be, since he is not in “good standing.” ( _BCO_ 43-1). Therefore, an appeal from his excommunication is the censured person’s last and only opportunity to seek relief from a censuring court that has made an error about whether he is truly “incorrigible and contumacious.” In deciding to elevate censure to excommunication it is possible for a court to act irregularly, refuse reasonable indulgence, receive improper evidence or decline to receive proper evidence, hurry to a decision, manifest prejudice, make a mistake, or commit injustice in the censure. ( _BCO_ 42-3). But if the censuring court’s actions are not regulated by the familiar and well-defined boundaries afforded by a case of process, how can the accused obtain, and the higher courts afford him, a meaningful review of his excommunication? The weightiness of this last opportunity for review is evident when we understand that once he is excommunicated, he thereafter lacks any kind of standing either to complain or appeal should the court of original jurisdiction refuse to restore him, thus instantiating and insulating any error of the censuring court, perhaps permanently. This proposed amendment to _BCO_ 30-4 provides that the court, having reckoned the case unfit for excommunication in the first instance, and having fulfilled its responsibility to “frequently converse with” the accused “as well as pray with him and for him, that it would please God to give him repentance” ( _BCO_ 37-2), must thereafter demonstrate that the censure of indefinite suspension from the Sacraments should be elevated because those peculiar conditions justifying the different and greater censure of excommunication (i.e., that the case involves a “gross crime or heresy” and that the offender has shown himself “incorrigible and contumacious”) have been established before taking the extraordinary step of “excising him from the communion of the Church.” _Adopted by the Southeast Alabama Presbytery at its stated meeting, April 22,_ _2025_ _Attested by TE Kevin Corley, stated clerk_

source: OVERTURE 39 from the Southeast Alabama Presbytery (to CCB, OC)
body: “Amend _BCO_ 34-8 and add _BCO_ 33-5 to Clarify the Process for Elevating Suspension from Office to Deposition” **Be it resolved** that _BCO_ 34-8 be amended as follows (underlining for additions; strikethrough for deletions): **34-8.** A minister under indefinite suspension from his office or deposed for scandalous conduct shall not be restored, even on the deepest sorrow for his sin, until he shall exhibit for a considerable time such an eminently exemplary, humble and edifying life and testimony as shall heal the wound made by his scandal. A deposed minister shall in no case be restored until it shall appear that the general sentiment of the Church is strongly in his favor, and demands his restoration; and then only by the court inflicting the censure, or with that court’s consent. The removal of deposition requires a three-fourths (3/4) vote of the court inflicting the censure, or a three-fourths (3/4) vote of the court to which the majority of the original court delegates that authority. Likewise, if it shall appear in time that any minister suspended from office fails to satisfy the requirements of _BCO_ 34-8 and/or _BCO_ 37-8, Presbytery may depose him from office, a majority of three-quarters (3/4) being necessary for this purpose. In such a case, the clerk shall under the order of the Presbytery forthwith deliver to the minister concerned a written note that, at the next stated meeting, the question of his being so dealt with is to be considered. This notice shall distinctly state the grounds for this proceeding. The party thus notified shall be heard in his own defense; and if the decision pass against him he may appeal, as if he had been tried after the usual forms. **Be it further resolved** that a new _BCO_ 33-5 be added as follows (underlining for new wording): **33-5.** When a ruling elder or deacon is indefinitely suspended from office after a case of process or a BCO 38-1 case without process, he shall not be restored, even on the deepest sorrow for his sin, until he shall exhibit for a considerable time such an eminently exemplary, humble and edifying life and testimony as shall heal any wound made by his scandal. The removal of deposition requires a three-fourths (3/4) vote of his Session. If it shall appear in time that any ruling elder or deacon suspended from office fails to satisfy the above requirements, the Session may depose him from office, a majority of threequarters (3/4) being necessary for this purpose. In such a case, the clerk shall under the order of the Session forthwith deliver to the Ruling Elder or Deacon concerned a written note that, at the next stated meeting, the question of his being so dealt with is to be considered. This notice shall distinctly state the grounds for this proceeding. The party thus notified shall be heard in his own defense; and if the decision pass against him he may appeal, as if he had been tried after the usual forms. So that _BCO_ 34-8 as amended would read: **34-8.** A minister under indefinite suspension from his office or deposed for scandalous conduct shall not be restored, even on the deepest sorrow for his sin, until he shall exhibit for a considerable time such an eminently exemplary, humble and edifying life and testimony as shall heal the wound made by his scandal. A deposed minister shall in no case be restored until it shall appear that the general sentiment of the Church is strongly in his favor and demands his restoration; and then only by the court inflicting the censure, or with that court’s consent. The removal of deposition requires a three-fourths (3/4) vote of the court inflicting the censure, or a three-fourths (3/4) vote of the court to which the majority of the original court delegates that authority. Likewise, if it shall appear in time that any minister suspended from office fails to satisfy the requirements of _BCO_ 34-8 and/or _BCO_ 37-8, Presbytery may depose him from office, a majority of three-quarters (3/4) being necessary for this purpose. In such a case, the clerk shall under the order of the Presbytery forthwith deliver to the minister concerned a written note that, at the next stated meeting, the question of his being so dealt with is to be considered. This notice shall distinctly state the grounds for this proceeding. The party thus notified shall be heard in his own defense; and if the decision pass against him he may appeal, as if he had been tried after the usual forms. So that _BCO_ 33-5 as amended would read: **33-5.** When a ruling elder or deacon is indefinitely suspended from office after a case of process or a BCO 38-1 case without process, he shall not be restored, even on the deepest sorrow for his sin, until he shall exhibit for a considerable time such an eminently exemplary, humble and edifying life and testimony as shall heal any wound made by his scandal. The removal of deposition requires a three-fourths (3/4) vote of his Session. If it shall appear in time that any ruling elder or deacon suspended from office fails to satisfy the above requirements, the Session may depose him from office, a majority of threequarters (3/4) being necessary for this purpose. In such a case, the clerk shall under the order of the Session forthwith deliver to the Ruling Elder or Deacon concerned a written note that, at the next stated meeting, the question of his being so dealt with is to be considered. This notice shall distinctly state the grounds for this proceeding. The party thus notified shall be heard in his own defense; and if the decision pass against him he may appeal, as if he had been tried after the usual forms. **RATIONALE:** Indefinite suspension from office is a distinct and insular censure of the Church ( _BCO_ 30-3) and is subject to review by the higher courts via appeal or complaint. By contrast, the procedural mechanism and kind of process applicable to _elevating_ indefinite suspension from office to deposition from office is less clear as has been demonstrated recently in the SJC case _TE Aaron Myers v._ _Iliana Presbytery_ ( _M51GA_, 2024, page 824) a swell as formerly in _Dallison v._ _North Florida Presbytery_ ( _M30GA_, 2002, page 156). It would therefore be wise for the Assembly to enact changes to our Rules of Discipline to promote clarity and uniformity regarding agreeable and appropriate procedures for elevating indefinite suspension from office to deposition from office. **Elevation of Censure to Deposition for Teaching Elders** With respect to teaching elders, indefinite suspension from office serves the Church to protect the integrity of the gospel ministry. Since a Presbytery may conclude that the continuance of a convicted minister in office would scandalize or otherwise hurt the Church (or even the minister), it may choose indefinite suspension, adopting a “wait and see” approach particularly where the Presbytery sees reasonable prospects for his repentance and restoration to the ministry. _BCO_ 37-8, governing the “Removal of Censure” in cases of suspension from office, mandates that the Presbytery “proceed with great caution,” advancing through deliberate stages of a gradual restoration, first admitting him to the Sacraments (if he was suspended from them), and only later giving him “the privilege of preaching on probation for a time, so as to test the sincerity of his repentance and prospect of his usefulness.” It continues, “When satisfied in these respects, the Presbytery shall take steps to restore him to his office,” noting that “the case shall always be under judicial consideration until the declaration of restoration has been pronounced. Notably, _BCO_ 37-8 prescribes no procedural mechanism defining what the phrase “take steps to restore him to his office” should entail, and there is no mention at all what procedural “steps” might be involved in _elevating_ his suspension from office to deposition from office. Additionally, _BCO_ 30-3 (“Church Censures”) prescribes, “In the case of indefinite suspension from office imposed due to scandalous conduct, the procedure outlined in _BCO_ 34-8 (“Special Rules Pertaining to Process Against a Minister”) shall be followed.” That provision says: A minister under indefinite suspension from his office or deposed for scandalous conduct shall not be restored, even on the deepest sorrow for his sin, until he shall exhibit for a considerable time such an eminently exemplary, humble and edifying life and testimony as shall heal the wound made by his scandal. It adds: A deposed minister shall in no case be restored until it shall appear that the general sentiment of the Church is strongly in his favor, and demands his restoration; and then only by the court inflicting the censure, or with that court’s consent. The removal of deposition requires a three-fourths (3/4) vote of the court inflicting the censure, or a three-fourths (3/4) vote of the court to which the majority of the original court delegates that authority. Interestingly, while _BCO_ 34-8 prescribes a procedural mechanism for restoration to office after deposition from office, it is frustratingly silent about what steps should be taken to either elevate suspension from office to deposition or to remove the same. Clearly, the duration of a minister’s indefinite suspension from office is related to the elevation of that censure to deposition, for once a minister is indefinitely suspended, he must either be restored in time or be deposed. There are no other options, and because the duration of the censure is presently governed by the various considerations described in _BCO_ 34-8 and _BCO_ 37-8, the particular facts and circumstances must guide the Presbytery’s judgment about how best to proceed. The question of a man’s deposition from the ministry is different in important ways from excommunication. A minister both suspended from office and the Sacraments might be deemed unsuitable to be restored to office yet remain a genuine Christian and therefore be restored to the Sacraments upon satisfactory evidence of repentance ( _BCO_ 36-5), sometimes well before his Presbytery finds it appropriate to restore him to the ministry. Elevating suspension from the Sacraments to excommunication as compared to elevating suspension from office to deposition is like comparing apples and oranges. Every Christian has a duty to repent of sin, but Christians have neither a manifest duty to be eligible for gospel ministry nor to pursue (or be restored to) the same. excommunication involves a determination that a man has committed the offense of being “incorrigible and contumacious” ( _BCO_ 30-4), matters regularly assessed in cases of process, but the determination of those factors governing whether a man should be restored to the ministry as we find them in _BCO_ 34-8 and _BCO_ 37-8 are not readily susceptible to adjudication in a case of process with the appointment of a prosecutor in the way that the refusal to repent of sin is, nor are the stakes as high since deposition from office does not remove a man from the communion of the Church. The situation of an indefinitely suspended minister, particularly as time marches on, is analogous to the irregularity we address in cases where a minister is “divested” from the ministry because he has been “without call” for an extended period as governed by _BCO_ 34-10. The key difference is that divestment “without censure” is expressly _not_ available to an indefinitely suspended minister because the cause of his ineligibility arises from his having committed an _offense_ rather than an inculpable “lack of acceptance to the Church.” This proposed amendment would adopt the general form of parliamentary procedure used in divestiture cases as the procedure governing the elevation of indefinite suspension from office to deposition from office which, while less formal than a case of process, is both tested and familiar, requiring notice to the suspended minister and an opportunity for him to be heard as well as a proposed …

source: OVERTURE 40 from the Southeast Alabama Presbytery (to CCB, OC)
body: “Amend _BCO_ 35-9 to Require Recording All Parts of a Trial” **Be it resolved** that the 52 [nd] General Assembly revise _BCO_ 35-9 as shown below (underlining for additions; strikethrough for deletions): **35-9.** All testimony parts of a trial other than deliberations shall be recorded (by transcription, audiotape, videotape, or some other electronic means) and witnesses informed of such prior to testifying. Such recording becomes part of the Record of the Case. However, in order to be referenced in written or oral briefs, such recording must be transcribed and the transcription authenticated by the trial court. The court of final appeal may assess the cost of transcription equitably among the parties So that _BCO_ 35-9 as amended would read: **35-9.** All parts of a trial other than deliberations shall be recorded (by transcription, audiotape, videotape, or some other electronic means) and witnesses informed of such prior to testifying. Such recording becomes part of the Record of the Case. However, in order to be referenced in written or oral briefs, such recording must be transcribed and the transcription authenticated by the trial court. The court of final appeal may assess the cost of transcription equitably among the parties **Rationale** 1. This clarifies, for example, that objections raised by the parties during a trial and the court's ruling on those objections, are recorded and available for transcription in the event of an appeal _Adopted by the Southeast Alabama Presbytery at its stated meeting, April 22,_ _2025_ _Attested by TE Kevin Corley, stated clerk_

source: OVERTURE 41 from the Calvary Presbytery (to AC)
body: “Direct the AC to Collect & Report Each Congregation’s Public Worship Service Times” **Whereas** the worship of God, and particularly the corporate public worship of God, is vital to the Christian faith ( _WLC_ 117); and, **Whereas** proper observance of the Fourth Commandment requires due diligence and preparation ( _WLC_ 121); and **Whereas** due diligence and preparation requires knowing when particular congregations will gather for public worship; and, **Whereas** the charge of keeping the Sabbath is more specially directed to superiors (WLC 118); and **Whereas** information about public worship service times are at present occasionally unavailable and often tedious for individuals to collect through publicly accessible channels; and, **Therefore, be it resolved** that the 52 [nd] General Assembly direct the Administrative Committee to collect and report each congregation’s public worship service times (inclusive of all stated worship services) on the church directory map available at https://www.pcaac.org/churchdirectory/. **Therefore, be it further resolved** that the 52 [nd] General Assembly encourage the Administrative Committee to seek the assistance of the several Presbyteries in this task. _Adopted by Calvary Presbytery at its stated meeting of April 24, 2025._ _Attested by /s/ RE Melton L. Duncan, Stated Clerk_

source: OVERTURE 42 from the Calvary Presbytery (to AC)
body: “Direct the Stated Clerk Not to Collect Statistical Data Pertaining to Age or Ethnicity” **Whereas** _RAO_ 4-11 authorizes the Administrative Committee to collect statistical information for the purpose of providing and publishing “guidelines for the Partnership Share Giving Program of the PCA, including the Ministry Ask” and for no other stated reason; and, **Whereas** _RAO_ 4-11 specifies that said “guidelines shall include statistical information expressed both in per capita giving terms and in proportional (percentage) giving terms to demonstrate the giving necessary to attain full funding for budgets of the General Assembly Committees and Agencies” and nothing more; and, **Whereas** the Office of the Stated Clerk, through a note contained ina box on the bottom of page 2 of the 2024 Annual Statistical Report Form, informed the congregations of the PCA that “two new line items” regarding “communicant member ethnicity and age” would appear “on the 2025 Annual Statistical Report Form” to be sent out for completion in 2026; and, **Whereas** the practical difficulties of collecting information on “communicant member ethnicity and age” are greater than perhaps the Stated Clerk’s Office has yet considered due to members’ reticence to share their ages or uncertain of how best to categorize their ethnicity, with many of our members being the children of interracial/multiethnic unions; and, **Whereas** the theological commitments of the PCA derived from Scripture and expressed in the PCA’s subordinate Standards and Constitute militate against the collection of data pertaining to ethnicity, for the PCA confesses with Scripture that though our members come from many different backgrounds (ethnic and otherwise), our Triune God has united us together as “one body” (1 Cor. 12:12), with Christ Himself being “our peace, who made both groups into one and broke down the barrier of the dividing wall” (Eph. 2:14), baptizing all “by one Spirit…into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves of free,” and making all “to drink of one Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:13), even while acknowledging that Old Testament historical narratives, ceremonial laws, and prophecies frequently refer to people groups by familial origin, tribal associations, ethnic affinities, nations, and what some commentators might refer to as racial distinctions, yet never in such a way so as to accept as appropriate the continuing use of such distinctions in the formal categorization of members of the church of Jesus Christ; and, **Whereas** the kingdoms of this world may collect (and even act upon) certain demographic information, yet God has neither directed nor authorized the church to collect such information pertaining to ethnicity; and, **Whereas** there are two classes of people with which the church should be concerned, in its formal statistical record-keeping: covenant-keepers and covenant-breakers ( _BCO_ 56-4.j.), recorded in the PCA as those who are in covenant with God through their own “profession of faith in Christ” ( _BCO_ 6-2; see also 57-3, 4) or “through the covenant and by right of birth” as “non-communing members of the church” ( _BCO_ 6-1), thus furnishing the church with two classes of those who are deemed in covenant with God—communing members and noncommuning members (WCF 25.2; WLC 62)—and one additional record of those who break covenant with God and come under the censure of excommunication ( _BCO_ 30-1, 4); and, **Whereas** there is no clear usefulness or theological justification for further subdividing either of these two categories (i.e., covenant-keepers and covenant-breakers) in terms of either age or ethnicity; and, **Whereas** the collection of data pertaining to age or ethnicity gives the appearance of the sins of partiality (James 2:9) and pride, which must not be indulged even at the first stirring of the same (James 1:14-15), as illustrated in King David’s sinful (and deadly) census recorded in 2 Samuel 24 and cited in 1 Chronicles 21; and, **Whereas** the resolution of the conflict between Hellenistic Jews and native Hebrews in Acts 6 does not constitute an approved example that would lead us by necessary inference to collect denomination-wide demographic data pertaining to ethnicity or age; and, **Whereas** the collection of demographic data pertaining to ethnicity or age is not necessary for the undershepherds called and ordained by Christ to know the flock in their care; and, **Whereas** the church is called to “examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; abstain from every form of evil” (1 Thess. 5:2122). **Therefore, be it resolved** that Calvary Presbytery hereby overtures the 52 [nd] General Assembly to direct the Office of the Stated Clerk through the Administrative Committee not to collect statistical data pertaining to age or ethnicity in annual statistical reports _Adopted by Calvary Presbytery at its stated meeting of April 24, 2025._ _Attested by /s/ RE Melton L. Duncan, Stated Clerk_

and, **Whereas** the Office of the Stated Clerk, through a note contained ina box on the bottom of page 2 of the 2024 Annual Statistical Report Form, informed the congregations of the PCA that “two new line items” regarding “communicant member ethnicity and age” would appear “on the 2025 Annual Statistical Report Form” to be sent out for completion in 2026; and, **Whereas** the practical difficulties of collecting information on “communicant member ethnicity and age” are greater than perhaps the Stated Clerk’s Office has yet considered due to members’ reticence to share their ages or uncertain of how best to categorize their ethnicity, with many of our members being the children of interracial/multiethnic unions; and, **Whereas** the theological commitments of the PCA derived from Scripture and expressed in the PCA’s subordinate Standards and Constitute militate against the collection of data pertaining to ethnicity, for the PCA confesses with Scripture that though our members come from many different backgrounds (ethnic and otherwise), our Triune God has united us together as “one body” (1 Cor. 12:12), with Christ Himself being “our peace, who made both groups into one and broke down the barrier of the dividing wall” (Eph. 2:14), baptizing all “by one Spirit…into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves of free,” and making all “to drink of one Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:13), even while acknowledging that Old Testament historical narratives, ceremonial laws, and prophecies frequently refer to people groups by familial origin, tribal associations, ethnic affinities, nations, and what some commentators might refer to as racial distinctions, yet never in such a way so as to accept as appropriate the continuing use of such distinctions in the formal categorization of members of the church of Jesus Christ; and, **Whereas** the kingdoms of this world may collect (and even act upon) certain demographic information, yet God has neither directed nor authorized the church to collect such information pertaining to ethnicity; and, **Whereas** there are two classes of people with which the church should be concerned, in its formal statistical record-keeping: covenant-keepers and covenant-breakers ( _BCO_ 56-4.j.), recorded in the PCA as those who are in covenant with God through their own “profession of faith in Christ” ( _BCO_ 6-2; see also 57-3, 4) or “through the covenant and by right of birth” as “non-communing members of the church” ( _BCO_ 6-1), thus furnishing the church with two classes of those who are deemed in covenant with God—communing members and noncommuning members (WCF 25.2; WLC 62)—and one additional record of those who break covenant with God and come under the censure of excommunication ( _BCO_ 30-1, 4); and, **Whereas** there is no clear usefulness or theological justification for further subdividing either of these two categories (i.e., covenant-keepers and covenant-breakers) in terms of either age or ethnicity; and, **Whereas** the collection of data pertaining to age or ethnicity gives the appearance of the sins of partiality (James 2:9) and pride, which must not be indulged even at the first stirring of the same (James 1:14-15), as illustrated in King David’s sinful (and deadly) census recorded in 2 Samuel 24 and cited in 1 Chronicles 21; and, **Whereas** the resolution of the conflict between Hellenistic Jews and native Hebrews in Acts 6 does not constitute an approved example that would lead us by necessary inference to collect denomination-wide demographic data pertaining to ethnicity or age; and, **Whereas** the collection of demographic data pertaining to ethnicity or age is not necessary for the undershepherds called and ordained by Christ to know the flock in their care; and, **Whereas** the church is called to “examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; abstain from every form of evil” (1 Thess. 5:2122). **Therefore, be it resolved** that Calvary Presbytery hereby overtures the 52 [nd] General Assembly to amend _RAO_ 4-11 by adding the following to the third paragraph (underlining for additions): Such statistical information shall not include data pertaining to age or ethnicity. So that the amended section will read as follows: **4-11.** The budget for each permanent Committee and Agency shall be submitted to the Administrative Committee of General Assembly, which shall independently evaluate the proposed budget of each permanent Committee and Agency and report to the Assembly its considered opinion on the adoption. To protect the ministry and fiduciary responsibilities of the Committees and Agency Boards, the financial coordination and independent evaluation of the budgets by the Administrative Committee shall be for review, discussion, and recommendation to the Assembly. Should modifications in budgets be deemed necessary by the Assembly, special care shall be taken that changes not be made in such a way as to threaten the continuity or effectiveness of the Committee’s or Agency’s ministry. Budgets of permanent Committees and Agencies that are agreed upon by the Administrative Committee may be changed only by a twothirds vote of the Assembly commissioners present and voting at the time the budget is submitted for adoption. In the event the Administrative Committee disagrees with the budget submitted by one of the Committees or Boards, in whole or any item thereof, the General Assembly may adopt either the Committee’s or Board’s budget or the Administrative Committee’s recommended budget by simple majority. The requirement of a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly applies only to changes not recommended by the Administrative Committee, initiated on the floor of the Assembly. With respect to the Committees and Agencies, financial coordination is through the Administrative Committee to the Assembly and from the General Assembly to the Committees and Agencies. The Administrative Committee is a “filter upward” and has no downward authority. The Administrative Committee shall annually provide and publish guidelines for the Partnership Share Giving Program of the PCA, including the Ministry Ask. These guidelines shall include statistical information expressed both in per capita giving terms and in proportional (percentage) giving terms to demonstrate the giving necessary to attain full funding for budgets of the General Assembly Committees and Agencies. Such statistical information shall not include data pertaining to age or ethnicity. The Committees and Agencies receiving support through the PCA Partnership Share Giving Program shall present their financial needs and their Ministry Ask to the Administrative Committee for review and recommendation in the course of the regular budgeting process. Each Committee and Agency shall then be free to request from the PCA churches and constituency the contributions necessary to fund its approved budget. While all churches remain free to give their contributions as they by God’s guidance determine, all churches are encouraged to give, as they are able, at least ten percent (10%) of their tithes and offerings to the PCA causes of presbyteries and General Assembly. The Administrative Committee shall maintain a manual containing the Affirmation of Core Financial Standards. This information, by which each PCA General Assembly ministry (Committee or Agency) shall function and by which the budget process is governed for each Committee and Agency, shall be available to all constituencies _Adopted by Calvary Presbytery at its stated meeting of April 24, 2025._ _Attested by /s/ RE Melton L. Duncan, Stated Clerk_

source: OVERTURE 44 from the Pee Dee Presbytery (to AC)
body: “Transition byFaith to a Press-Release-Based Publication” **Whereas** byFaith magazine was established as the official publication of the Presbyterian Church in America (PCA) to serve as a voice for the denomination; and **Whereas** the PCA is committed to maintaining a clear distinction between denominational communications and editorial commentary, ensuring that official communications remain impartial and representative of the church as a whole; and **Whereas** the purpose of denominational communication should be to provide clear and accurate information regarding the actions, policies, and ministries of the PCA without editorializing or presenting particular viewpoints that may not reflect the consensus of the denomination (1 Corinthians 14:40); and **Whereas** byFaith magazine has, at times, functioned as more than a source of official denominational news, engaging in commentary and editorial perspectives that may not always represent the collective voice of the General Assembly ( _BCO_ 14-1.5; _WCF_ 31.3); and **Whereas** many churches and Presbyteries would benefit from an official PCA publication that focuses on disseminating essential information, press releases, and updates from ministries and Presbyteries in a way that prioritizes clarity, transparency, and denominational unity (Ephesians 4:3); and **Whereas** transitioning byFaith into a press-release-based platform would enhance trust in denominational communications by ensuring that its content remains neutral, factual, and reflective of the entire PCA rather than selective viewpoints; and **Whereas** such transition and narrowing of focus would be accompanied by a decrease in expenditures for byFaith, which currently is ~$400,000 ( _M51GA_, 2024, Appendix A, 139), assisting the Administrative Committee in meeting its budget; and **Whereas** the reputation of Christ and His Church should not be compromised by unnecessary controversies or unbalanced representation in denominational communications (2 Corinthians 8:21); **Therefore, be it resolved** that the 52 [nd] General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America directs the Administrative Committee to transition byFaith magazine from its current editorial format to a press-releasebased publication, limited to the following types of content: 1. Official press releases from the Administrative Committee and other denominational agencies regarding actions taken by the General Assembly, significant initiatives, and denominational decisions. 2. Ministry updates from PCA churches, Presbyteries, and denominational agencies, highlighting the work of the church in missions, discipleship, and service. 3. Announcements and reports from the General Assembly and Presbyteries, ensuring transparency and accessibility of denominational proceedings. **Be it further resolved** that the Administrative Committee develop and implement a plan to restructure byFaith within one year of the adoption of this overture, ensuring that the new format aligns with the PCA’s commitment to truth, transparency, and denominational unity _Adopted by the Pee Dee Presbytery at its stated meeting, April 26, 2025_ _Attested by TE Mark Horne, Stated Clerk_

source: OVERTURE 45 from the Hills and Plains Presbytery (to MNA)
body: “Change the Boundaries of Covenant and Hills & Plains Presbyteries” _**OVERTURE 21 WITHDRAWN BY COVENANT PRESBYTERY**_ **Whereas**, the general guidelines for dividing Presbyteries approved by the 41 [st] General Assembly of the PCA state “Presbytery boundaries should be such that her member churches have a common commitment to the region within their boundaries and a deep commitment to their shared responsibility to cover the region with the Gospel through evangelism and church planting.” **Whereas**, the same general guidelines for dividing presbyteries further state “A Presbytery should have regional cohesiveness. The Presbytery should have a geographical spread that is as reasonable as possible to facilitate planting churches, encouraging fellowship, participating together in shared ministry and conducting the necessary business of the Presbytery.” **Whereas**, the 16 [th] General Assembly of the PCA adopted guidelines for Presbytery boundaries stating, “A presbytery should have a radius of 2 1/2 hours maximum driving distance.” **Whereas**, Sebastian County, Arkansas, where Covenant Presbyterian Church of Fort Smith is located on the farthest western border of Covenant Presbytery and is adjacent to the border of Hills & Plains Presbytery, and **Whereas**, the Session of Covenant Presbyterian Church of Fort Smith wants to regularly attend Presbytery meetings but finds it difficult at times due to extended travel, and **Whereas**, the locations of the stated meetings of Hills & Plains Presbytery are much closer to Fort Smith than the stated meetings of Covenant Presbytery, and **Whereas**, the Session of Covenant Presbyterian Church of Fort Smith, Arkansas has petitioned Covenant Presbytery and Hills & Plains Presbytery to so act, **Now therefore, be it resolved** that Hills and Plains Presbytery, in concurrence with the Session of Covenant Presbyterian Church of Fort Smith and Covenant Presbytery, overtures the 2025 General Assembly to transfer Sebastian, Scott, Crawford, Franklin, Johnson, Logan, and Polk counties from the geographic bounds of Covenant Presbytery to the geographic bounds of Hills and Plains Presbytery, and that Covenant Presbyterian Church of Fort Smith and her Teaching Elder(s) be received into the membership of Hills and Plains Presbytery. _Adopted by the Hills and Plains Presbytery at its stated meeting, May 6,_ _2025_ _Attested by /s/ TE Aaron Raines, stated clerk_

source: OVERTURE 46 from the Metro Atlanta Presbytery (to MNA)
body: “Change the Boundaries of Georgia Foothills and Metro Atlanta Presbyteries” **Whereas** Lumpkin County, GA is the farthest northern point of Metro Atlanta Presbytery; and **Whereas** it lies geographically in the northeast Georgia mountains, near many churches within the current boundary of Georgia Foothills Presbytery; and **Whereas** Georgia Foothills Presbytery desires to start an RUF campus ministry at University of North Georgia located in the city of Dahlonega in Lumpkin County; and **Whereas** the Session of Creekstone Church, the only PCA church located in Lumpkin County, is agreeable to come into Georgia Foothills Presbytery; and **Whereas** the minutes of the 46 [th] General Assembly established the boundary of Georgia Foothills Presbytery to be the Georgia counties of Hall, Barrow, Jackson, Clarke, Oconee, Habersham, and Union counties; also the counties of Oglethorpe, Elbert, Madison, Hart, Franklin, Banks, White, Stephens, Rabun, and Towns; and Gwinnett county north of the defined boundaries, from east to west, of Highway 316, then Sugarloaf Parkway to Peachtree Industrial Boulevard, then an imaginary line westward from the intersection of Peachtree Industrial Boulevard and Sugarloaf Parkway to the Chattahoochee River; and **Whereas** the minutes of the 46 [th] General Assembly established the boundary of Metro Atlanta Presbytery to be the Georgia counties of Dekalb, Fulton, Clayton, Cobb (East of I-75), Dawson, Lumpkin, Coweta, Heard, Spalding, Troup, Merriweather, Pike, Fayette, Forsyth, Rockdale, Newton, Henry, and Walton; and Gwinnett county south of the defined boundaries, from east to west, of Highway 316, then Sugarloaf Parkway to Peachtree Industrial Boulevard, then an imaginary line westward from the intersection of Peachtree Industrial Boulevard and Sugarloaf Parkway to the Chattahoochee River; **Therefore be it resolved** that Metro Atlanta Presbytery overtures the 52 [nd] General Assembly as follows: - That Lumpkin County be transferred from Metro Atlanta Presbytery to Georgia Foothills Presbytery; - By adding Lumpkin County to the list of Georgia counties included within the boundary of Georgia Foothills Presbytery; and - By removing Lumpkin County from the list of Georgia counties included within the boundary of Metro Atlanta Presbytery. _Adopted by the Metro Atlanta Presbytery at its stated meeting, May 6, 2025_ _Attested by TE Randy Schlichting, stated clerk_

source: OVERTURE 47 from the Great Lakes Presbytery (to OC, AC)
body: “Erect Ad Interim Committee on Christian Nationalism **Whereas**, there is a question whether those that hold to the Historic _WCF_ (1647) concerning the magistrate ( _WCF_ 23-3) need to take an exception because of differences from the version of the _WCF_ adopted by the PCA (1788); and **Whereas**, some in the PCA have labeled the historic _WCF_ ’s views concerning the magistrate as a form of Christian Nationalism; and **Whereas**, some also hold to a version of Christian Nationalism that they describe as Ethno-Nationalism, or label themselves as Heritage Americans; and **Whereas**, those that hold these teachings profess conformity to the Reformed Tradition; and **Whereas**, these have caused confusion, division, and dissension even among the congregants of PCA churches and affected PCA pastors and officers; and **Whereas**, church courts have the responsibility to determine questions of doctrine seriously, and in general to maintain truth and righteousness, condemning erroneous opinions which tend to bring injury to the eace, purity, or progress of the Church ( _BCO_ 11-4); **Therefore, be it resolved** that the 52 [nd] PCA General Assembly erect and convene an Ad Interim Study Committee on Christian Nationalism ( _RAO_ 9-1), to study the relationship between Christian Nationalism, Ethno-Nationalism, and related teachings. Further, the committee shall advise on whether these teachings and formulations are in conformity with the system of doctrine taught in the _Westminster_ _Standards_ or where they may diverge from the system of doctrine. **Further**, the committee shall write a report that gives pastoral guidance when addressing congregations, new members, and future officers of the PCA. **Be it further resolved** that the General Assembly’s Moderator be empowered as a commission to populate the ad interim committee with three (3) Teaching Elders and four (4) Ruling Elders. **Be it further resolved** that the budget for the study committee be set at $10,000/year and that funds be derived from gifts to the AC designated for that purpose, with the General Assembly appealing to the various Presbyteries to fund this initiative via such gifts ( _RAO_ 9-3). **Be it further resolved** that the Great Lakes Presbytery is committed to offer a $1,000 gift to assist in funding the work of this Ad Interim Study Committee. _Adopted by the Great Lakes Presbytery at its stated meeting, May 3, 2025_ _Attested by TE Ryan Potter, stated clerk_

source: OVERTURE 48 from the Tennessee Valley Presbytery (to OC, AC)
body: “Erect an Ad Interim Committee for a Pastoral Letter on Christian Citizenship and Church-State Relations” **Whereas,** the duties of Christian citizenship are often disputed and prove perennially difficult for both elders and church members to discern; and **Whereas**, confusion exists about the proper relation between church and state; and **Whereas**, due to recent movements, publications, popular teachings, political strife, and societal stresses, the need for guidance concerning Christian citizenship and church-state relations has intensified; and **Whereas**, the _Westminster Standards_, as adopted by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Preface to the Presbyterian Church in America’s _Book of Church Order_ provide substantial, biblical guidance concerning Christian citizenship and the relationship of the church to the state; and **Whereas**, an explication of principles may prove more helpful than a focus on persons or rapidly changing movements, and may be helpful to the church in decades to come, **Therefore, be it resolved** that the 52 [nd] General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America direct its moderator to appoint an unfunded ad interim committee to produce a pastoral letter [45] or short paper applying the doctrine of the Constitution of the Presbyterian Church in America to questions of Christian citizenship and church-state relations for the edification of the Church. The committee will be composed of four teaching elders and three ruling elders and will set its own procedures and timelines. _Adopted by the Tennessee Valley Presbytery at its stated meeting, May 10,_ _2025_ _Attested by TE Ryan Frank Biese, stated clerk_ 45 An example of a previous PCA pastoral letter: [https://www.pcahistory.org/documents/pastoralletter.html](http://www.pcahistory.org/documents/pastoralletter.html)

source: OVERTURE 49 from the Pacific Northwest Presbytery (to OC, AC, CC,
body: CDM, CTS, Geneva, MNA, MTW, PCAF, RH, RUF) “Erect an ad interim committee on AI” **Be it resolved** that the General Assembly erect a study committee of seven members, consisting of teaching or ruling elders, with an annual budget of $15,000 (funded by gifts to the Administrative Committee), tasked to: a. Write a report by the 54th General Assembly (June 2027) on the teaching of Scripture and the _Westminster Standards_, with a particular reference to our anthropology ( _WCF_ 4, 7) and ecclesiology ( _WCF_ 25), and suggest general principles for the use or limits of artificial intelligence technology (AI) in the Church; b. Then apply these general principles to the following suggested areas: i. _Pastoral Ministry_ : AI use in preaching, teaching, and pastoral care ii. _Church Administration_ : AI use in local churches, Presbyteries, and the General Assembly, also addressing security concerns iii. _Church Discipline_ : suggest criteria for assessing AIgenerated evidence in church courts, especially in disciplinary cases iv. _Christian Vocation and Diaconal Ministry_ : a Reformed approach to work and service amid AI-driven changes in the workplace and economy, with diaconal strategies for affected church members v. _Christian Education:_ implications for PCA institutions (e.g., Covenant College, Covenant Seminary), especially on education philosophy and practice vi. _Medical Ethics_ : boundaries for AI use in medical practice with particular emphasis in recovering natural function vs. enhancing human ability beyond natural limitations vii. _Evangelism and Apologetics_ : strategies to proclaim the gospel and encourage Christian discipleship in contrast to AI-influenced ideologies (i.e., transhumanism, etc.) viii. _Ethical Issues_ : copyrighted materials illicitly used to train AIs; the impact of over-use of energy and water by server farms on poor communities; the use of AI to create simulated relationship and pornography ix. Any other significant applications the committee finds during this study. c. Consult theological, technical, or legal specialists as needed to aid in this study d. Propose amendments to the _Book of Church Order_ ( _BCO_ ) or changes to agency policies, if warranted by their findings. **Be it further resolved** that all General Assembly permanent committees, commissions, and agencies submit a report to the study committee within six months (December 31, 2025) specifying their current and proposed AI usage to help inform the study committee, and include that report in their annual reports to the 53th General Assembly (June 2026). **Rationale** The revolutionary character of artificial intelligence technology (AI) is already having an inevitable impact on every aspect of society and therefore on the Church and individual Christian living. AI presents opportunities and challenges requiring a serious engagement grounded within our confessional heritage. Scripture and our Standards affirm God’s sovereignty over all creation, the sufficiency of Scripture to guide to our faith and practice, and our call to exercise dominion with wisdom, which includes taking responsibility for technological innovations and their intended or unintended effects. AI’s growing influence is wide-reaching, ranging from sermon or educational preparation tools to major career realignments to potential “deepfake” evidence, and many other areas. It impacts pastoral and church ministry, Christian vocation and education, apologetic confrontations with new ideologies, significant impacts on the quality of human relationships, and other ethical and theological questions that need attention. There is a serious risk of losing critical thinking, knowledge, and wisdom as such skills are surrendered to AI. The PCA must shepherd its members and proclaim the gospel faithfully amidst these rapid changes, and a modest investment of $15,000 annually can enable a study to help the church with a biblical guide for their christian witness under these new conditions. _Adopted by the Pacific Northwest Presbytery at its stated meeting, May 9,_ _2025_ _Attested by TE Jerid Krulish, stated clerk_

source: OVERTURE 50 from the Chesapeake Presbytery (to OC)
body: “Encouragement to Discernment and Compassion regarding Immigrants” **Whereas**, Scripture commands believers to submit to and pray for governing authorities as instituted by God for the good of society and the restraint of evil (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17; 1 Timothy 2:1–2); and **Whereas**, the moral law of God, revealed in both Old and New Testaments, calls for the protection of human life and the care of the vulnerable— including the fatherless, the widow, the sojourner, and the oppressed (Exodus 22:21; Deuteronomy 10:18–19; Proverbs 31:8–9; Matthew 25:35–40); and **Whereas**, the _Westminster Larger Catechism_ teaches that the sixth commandment requires “all careful studies, and lawful endeavors, to preserve the life of ourselves and others” ( _WLC_ Q.135), and forbids “the neglecting or withdrawing the lawful and necessary means of preservation of life” ( _WLC_ Q.136); and **Whereas**, the Lord Jesus Himself was once a political refugee, having fled as an infant with His parents into Egypt to escape the violent policies of Herod (Matthew 2:13–15), and He taught that welcoming the stranger is integral to the life of discipleship (Matthew 25:35–36); and **Whereas**, many immigrants in the United States have entered due to political instability, persecution, or extreme poverty, and live peacefully and productively in our communities—often without access to legal status—yet remain vulnerable to exploitation, fear, and injustice; and **Whereas**, God's law commands compassion and justice for the sojourner: “You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him… You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself” (Exodus 22:21; Leviticus 19:34); and **Whereas**, the people of God are themselves former aliens, now brought near by the blood of Christ, and made one new humanity in Him (Ephesians 2:12–19); and **Whereas**, Christ commissioned His Church to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:18–20), and Scripture affirms that God's saving purposes include all people—immigrants, refugees, and sojourners among them (Isaiah 56:6–8; Revelation 7:9–10); and **Whereas**, Acts 17:26-27 states that God allows the movement of people “so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him,”; and **Whereas**, God is bringing the nations to us, many of whom are Christians or likely to become Christians, according to missiologists; and **Whereas**, the 5 [th] and 14 [th] Amendments to the Constitution of our nation were added to ensure due process protections for all those living within its boundaries, and informing persons of how they can avail themselves of those due process protections is good and just; **Therefore be it resolved** that the Church should view immigrants, regardless of documentation status, primarily as neighbors and image-bearers whom Christ has called us to love, evangelize, disciple, and enfold into His body; and **Be it further resolved**, that the 52 [nd] General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America encourages all churches, Presbyteries, officers, and members to exercise gospel-informed discernment and compassion in responding to their new neighbors, including refugees, immigrants, asylum seekers, international students, and those currently without legal documentation; and **Be it further resolved**, that churches and members of the PCA be exhorted to respect and pray for civil authorities (1 Timothy 2:1–2), obey just laws (Romans 13:1–7), and encourage immigrants toward legal pathways when available, while also recognizing the divine mandate to preserve life, show mercy, and seek justice (Micah 6:8; Proverbs 31:8–9); and **Be it further resolved**, that PCA churches be encouraged to offer tangible care and support to immigrants—including compassionate outreach, ESL tutoring, vocational assistance, legal aid referrals, and inclusion in church fellowship—recognizing them as image-bearers of God and neighbors in need; and **Be it further resolved**, that the PCA encourages its churches to speak and act toward the sojourner in ways shaped not by political rhetoric but by the gospel, remembering our own identity as once-strangers, now brought near by grace (Ephesians 2:13); and **Be it further resolved**, that the PCA affirm the call to love, evangelize, disciple, and enfold immigrants into the body of Christ, remembering that the Great Commission includes all nations and peoples— regardless of legal status—as worthy recipients of the gospel of grace (Matthew 28:19–20; Isaiah 56:8; Revelation 7:9); and **Be it further resolved**, that when our churches and agencies interact with individuals who have no valid legal pathway to attain legal immigrant status, we should exercise pastoral wisdom by advising them to obey US immigrant laws, which might include voluntarily departing the US for their home country, or if this would be life-threatening, to a nation (if any) that might allow them legal residence; and **Be it finally resolved**, that the PCA commends to all believers a life of faithful citizenship—honoring authority, paying taxes, and living peaceably (Romans 13:6–7; 1 Peter 2:12)—while also walking courageously in obedience to God (Acts 5:29), bearing witness to the love, justice, and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ. _Adopted by the Chesapeake Presbytery at its stated meeting, May 13, 2025_ _Attested by TE Donald M. Dove_ _, stated clerk_
